#114393. 7 Ultrarunning Lessons Des Linden Learned from Her 100-Mile Debut

📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1548 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Trailrunnermag ↗ Open Full Page

7 Ultrarunning Lessons Des Linden Learned from Her 100-Mile Debut

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1548 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Trailrunnermag

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that andy Cochrane and Nick Danielson were on the ground outside of Fountain Hills, Arizona, on October 31 to document Des Linden’s 100-mile debut at the Javelina Jundred.
  • Despite Des Linden returning to Javelina Jundred “jeadquarters” five minutes ahead of schedule and in first place, I was worried.
  • Recent findings suggest that being a freelance filmmaker feels a bit like being a mercenary: One moment you have no aims for the rest of the year, and the next, you’re hopping in a rental van and rallying across the Southwest during a historic October storm to get to the next job.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that andy Cochrane and Nick Danielson were on the ground outside of Fountain Hills, Arizona, on October 31 to document Des Linden’s 100-mile debut at the Javelina Jundred. They bore witness to her exceptional first 60 miles, during which she took the lead in under-course-record pace, all the way through to her gritting out the remaining 40 miles to a ninth-place finish. They spoke with Linden after the race to find out what she learned—and why she’s already angling to come back.

Despite Des Linden returning to Javelina Jundred “jeadquarters” five minutes ahead of schedule and in first place, I was worried. I had followed her for the final half mile, camera rolling as her leg visibly seized up, likely from cramping. She had run 60 miles at course record pace, but still had forty to go—a long way without a fully functioning lower half. Linden sat on a chair and talked through the situation with her crew. A shoe switch, a lot more electrolytes, and roll the dice. Before I get into how the rest of her race played out, let me back up.

Recent findings suggest that being a freelance filmmaker feels a bit like being a mercenary: One moment you have no aims for the rest of the year, and the next, you’re hopping in a rental van and rallying across the Southwest during a historic October storm to get to the next job. This is exactly what my business partner Nick and I did after getting the call to document Des Linden’s first 100-mile race at the Javelina Jundred on October 31.

Industry observers note that after landing in Salt Lake City, we picked up a camper van from Roadsurfer, threw our bags in the back, and headed south on I-15. A quick stop in Moab for a 50K race of our own was followed by four days evading floods and trying to figure out which desert roads were impassable after the recent downpours—which turned out to be pretty good foretelling for the race itself.

It has been revealed that on the three previous occasions we’ve attended this event, it has been a delightful closing chapter to the season; Javelina has served as a sort of reward for making it to the end of our race coverage for the year, where the burden of logistics is removed from the job of filming. Instead of chasing athletes across the dirt roads of the Sierra Nevada at the Western States 100 or around a heavily glaciated massif at UTMB, the athletes at Javelina run in circles back to you. Five circles, to be exact. Adding to the enjoyment factor, Javelina is typically a giant Halloween party with racers and spectators dressed in costume under the warm desert sun.

In a recent development, however, this year was a little different. Deluge after deluge in the 24 hours leading up to the race saturated the race course. The sky relented just before the gun went off, but by the time the race had ended, over two more inches of precipitation had fallen. Not exactly what you expect for an event in the arid Sonoran Desert outside Phoenix, Arizona, but that’s why we love ultrarunning.

Industry observers note that we did our best to keep the cameras dry and our bodies warm as we followed Linden on her third ultra—well, fourth, if you count the road 50K world record. Despite a stunning road running resume, Linden was quick to point out that she’s still a newbie at trails and ultras but is excited to keep learning. Javelina’s first three laps were nearly perfect. But soon after her body shut down it was a struggle to make it to the finish line. At one point she had to stop for almost an hour, sitting and stretching until her legs finally relaxed and let her move again. And move again she did: Linden finished her first 100-miler as the ninth woman in 16:58:01, about three hours off winner Heather Jackson. We sat down with her the day after the race to learn her biggest lessons from the process.

According to recent reports, linden’s biggest takeaway from Javelina is to treat 100-milers, no matter the course, weather, or circumstances, with a ton of humility. Because they ask so much of your mind and body and are a completely unique style of racing, you can’t race a 100-miler like any other distance. “Just like when I started marathons,” Linden said, “I learned that if you’re cavalier with how you race it, you’ll pay the price at some point.”.

According to recent reports, linden was patient on her first 20-mile lap, sitting a few minutes back from the leaders. Feeling good, she picked up the pace on the next two laps, picking off all of the ladies in front of her to take the lead around the halfway mark. By the time she made it to the end of the third loop at mile 60, she had a six-minute gap on second—but her legs were starting to cramp.

Industry observers note that survival rapidly became the goal of lap four and the best way to do that was by listening to her pacer, Magda Boulet. Thankfully, there is no one on planet Earth better suited for the job. Boulet, a fellow U.S. Olympian in the marathon, is also a Western States winner and president of GU Energy Labs. She helped coax Linden forward, made sure she kept fueling, and stuck with her through all the ups and downs.

One of Linden’s biggest challenges in the transition from road to trails and marathons to ultras is how much she needs to consume during a race—and how hard it is to catch up if she falls behind. At Javelina, Linden took most of her calories and carbs with fluids, drinking three half-liter (500 mL) bottles each lap. This fueling strategy was developed for the typical heat of Javelina, but still worked well, as daytime temps almost hit 80 degrees Fahrenheit with 100% humidity.

Industry observers note that unfortunately, it wasn’t enough to keep her lower body from cramping around mile 60, which forced her to stop and stretch many times on the fourth lap. That setback resulted in her giving up the lead and ultimately the chance to win the race. “The fueling game has changed the sport,” Linden said. “You see it on the roads, but especially here. It’s something I will keep working on, probably forever.”.

It has been revealed that assuming Javelina would be hot and dry like just about every other year, Linden packed for those conditions, putting her focus on cooling strategies and nutrition for the heat. She expected hardpack trails and excruciatingly hot sun, but the weather gods had other looks. Heavy rain required Linden and her crew to scramble to find key pieces of gear, including a raincoat. And because lap four took much longer than expected, Linden ran the last couple miles of it after the sun set, sans headlamp.

Recent findings suggest that next time she’ll prepare for worst-case scenarios, but will also understand when to pull the plug. “You need to know when to be tough and when it’s enough,” Linden said. “If I had to do another lap, I would have been on the edge of hypothermia and the trails were so, so slippery. There is nothing wrong with saving it for another day, but also great value in staying tough.”.

Recent findings suggest that pacing strategy is different at every ultra, but there are some broad themes that apply to the majority of runners and racers, especially for someone with Linden’s ability to close in the back half if she’s feeling good. Surprisingly, this is similar to how she used to strategize for marathons. The first third should feel easy, the middle third is about keeping the pace steady, and the final third is when the racing begins. “The first three or even three-and-a-half laps are transportation,”  Linden stated, “the final lap or two is about racing.”.

Recent findings suggest that when things got hard for Linden on the final two laps, she leaned into her crew to get to the finish. After a lap with Boulet, Linden picked up her husband Ryan as a pacer. He’s one of the most positive and energetic people you’ll ever meet, and his positivity and drive—paired with a little patience—helped get her through heavy rain and strong winds in the last 20 miles.

Her main support at Javelina HQ was Charlie Lawrence, the 100K world record holder and good friend. “A crew that knows you well, knows the sport well, and knows the emotional ups and downs of 100 miles is a real difference maker,” Linden remarked. “I was excited to be around everyone all week, so it was good energy going into the race, which is key.”.

While Linden isn’t sure what the future holds or what her race calendar will look like next year, she walked away from the race with a surprising feeling. “I 100% want to come back to Javelina, it feels like unfinished business,” Linden mentioned. “I didn’t think it would be this clear, but I know I can do so much better here.”.

#114392. Tech Report: Senate Passes BAAJA, the Massive Permitting Bill That Will Expedite Development on Public Lands

Tech Report: Senate Passes BAAJA, the Massive Permitting Bill That Will Expedite Development on Public Lands

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (675 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A controversial bill aimed at speeding up infrastructure projects on public lands passed the U.S.
  • The Senate declined to vote on a flurry of last-minute amendments to the nearly 500-page text of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act — including one that would have banned data centers on public land, before voting for the third time late Thursday night.
  • Related: Senate Poised to Vote on Affordability Package that Hunters, Anglers Worry Is a Trojan Horse for Public-Land Rollbacks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A controversial bill aimed at speeding up infrastructure projects on public lands passed the U.S. Senate Thursday night and now heads to the House.

The Senate declined to vote on a flurry of last-minute amendments to the nearly 500-page text of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act — including one that would have banned data centers on public land, before voting for the third time late Thursday night. Support in the Senate eroded over the series of votes, from 73-25 on the first vote Nov. 9 to a final vote of 62-33. A bill requires a simple majority of 51 votes in the Senate to pass.

Related: Senate Poised to Vote on Affordability Package that Hunters, Anglers Worry Is a Trojan Horse for Public-Land Rollbacks.

Industry observers note that BAAJA is co-sponsored by Sen. Martin Heinrich, a Democrat from Upcoming Mexico often considered a conservation champion, and Sen. Mike Lee, the Utah Republican and architect of recent attempts to sell public land. Heinrich notes BAAJA cuts red tape and will speed up renewable energy projects to help fight climate change, increase jobs, and bring down energy costs for average Americans.

It has been revealed that conservation advocates, however, fear it will also lock in projects many sportsmen and women have spent years fighting, like a copper-sulfide mine by the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness or the Pebble Mine in Alaska’s Bristol Bay. It also may well open the door for massive data centers on public land, something most of the conservation and sporting community resoundingly oppose.

“I understand this is a big, bipartisan bill — it has some things in it I would rather it not have. But I negotiated the deal based on what was actually possible to get signed into law,” Heinrich wrote in an email to Outdoor Life earlier this week.

In a recent development, BAAJA proponents say it increases project certainty. Right now, one administration can reverse or cancel permits approved by a prior administration. But by limiting the back and forth between administrations the bill also drastically changes how much oversight a project can receive, even under foundational laws like the Endangered Species Act, Clean Water Act and National Historic Preservation Act. The bill will also limit public input into projects and judicial overview.

Many of the nation’s tribes have forcefully spoken out against the bill saying it severely curtails tribal input.

“Overall, the bill, by weakening these bedrock laws, would make it far easier to fast-track AI data centers as well as fossil fuel, mining, and other extractive infrastructure. Once these projects are approved, they would be difficult to unwind,” according to the Western Environmental Law Center. “BAAJA would cause grave, generational harm to the West’s public lands, waters and wildlife, and communities.”.

Heinrich has remarked he opposes data centers on public land.

It has been revealed that “To be clear, BAAJA is federal legislation focused on energy infrastructure and grid connectivity,” a spokesperson told OL in an emailed satement. “It does not ‘permit’ data centers on public lands. State and local government approval is still required. The Senator’s legislation addresses the federal energy infrastructure challenges associated with a grid that cannot keep up with demand; it does not circumvent the state and local processes that determine whether specific projects move forward.”.

Even conservation groups who support portions of the bill question how fast such a massive piece of legislation is moving through Congress. This is the first major permitting reform bill in decades and was introduced Sept. 30.

Read Next: Public-Land Sales, Energy Dominance, and Data Centers: What Interior’s Master Blueprint Really Means for Outdoorsmen.

In a recent development, the bill now heads to the House. If representatives make any changes to the Senate version, the Senate must vote again on the bill before it heads to President Trump’s desk for his signature. The president has stated he supports the bill.

Recent findings suggest that this story was updated on Nov. 20 at 2:30 p.m. CST to include comment from Sen. Heinrich’s office.

#114389. Industry News: NOAA Just Tweaked Its Winter Forecast. Here’s What’s Changed for Skiers.

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (660 w)

General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Skimag ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: NOAA Just Tweaked Its Winter Forecast. Here’s What’s Changed for Skiers.

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (660 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Skimag

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) has some encouraging news for skiers hoping for a major rebound after last winter’s dismal snow season, particularly in California and the Southwest.
  • According to recent reports, the agency’s Climate Prediction Center released its latest winter outlook on Thursday, Nov.
  • Sources indicate that the new forecast tweaks a few things from its previous iterations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Photo: Courtesy of Taos Ski Valley).

The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) has some encouraging news for skiers hoping for a major rebound after last winter’s dismal snow season, particularly in California and the Southwest.

According to recent reports, the agency’s Climate Prediction Center released its latest winter outlook on Thursday, Nov. 19, updating its forecast for the months ahead. The biggest development? The odds of above-average precipitation have increased across California and the Desert Southwest, offering a more promising outlook for a couple of the ski regions that have struggled with snow in recent years.

Sources indicate that the new forecast tweaks a few things from its previous iterations. Here’s a cheat sheet, but be sure to read on for more specifics and a regional breakdown:.

Recent findings suggest that finally, NOAA states that the upcoming precipitation forecasts are more reliable than their temperature forecasts this winter, which they attribute to the strong El Niño and an active southern storm track. In other words, there will be moisture, but there’s no guarantee it’ll come down as snow.

Here’s what the updated outlook says:.

The latest outlook favors above-average precipitation across the southern United States, stretching from southwestern Oregon and California through the Desert Southwest and into the southern Plains and Southeast.

Sources indicate that for ski country, California and the Southwest stand out. NOAA increased the probabilities of above-average precipitation in both regions compared with its previous outlook. Southern California and southwestern Arizona now have greater than a 60 percent chance of finishing the December-through-February period wetter than average.

That could be welcome news for resorts in the Sierra Nevada, including Mammoth and the Lake Tahoe region, as well as Arizona Snowbowl and Newly introduced Mexico’s Taos Ski Valley and Ski Santa Fe. The forecast also offers some encouragement for southern Colorado, including Purgatory, Wolf Creek, and Telluride, although it’s far less clear for the Front Range and Northern Rockies.

It’s worth noting here that NOAA is forecasting total precipitation, not snowfall, per se. Whether that moisture falls as snow or rain will depend on temperatures, snow levels, and where individual storms track. Still, a wetter-than-average winter would be a step in the right direction.

It has been revealed that NOAA continues to favor below-average precipitation across parts of the northern Rockies. The region also faces an increased likelihood of higher than average temperatures, a combo that’s not music to the ears of resorts in Montana, Idaho, and Wyoming. The Pacific Northwest also faces odds of warmer-than-average temperatures, particularly across Washington and Oregon.

Recent findings suggest that elsewhere, the outlook favors wetter-than-average conditions across much of the East Coast and Southeast. However, warmer temperatures could complicate snowfall prospects, particularly at lower-elevation ski areas.

Industry observers note that this is the latest chapter in a winter forecast that skiers have been watching closely for months. Earlier this summer, NOAA’s increasingly confident projections of a potentially historic El Niño raised hopes for a snowy rebound across parts of the West following last season’s exceptionally poor conditions.

In a recent development, in July, SKI spoke with meteorologists and ski-travel experts about what the developing climate pattern could mean for the upcoming season. The early consensus pointed toward the Southwest, particularly southern Colorado, New Mexico, Arizona, and California, as regions with favorable odds for an active storm track. Much of that remains the same.

It has been revealed that but there were plenty of question marks, and there still are, namely what will happen in central Colorado and Utah. NOAA’s earlier outlook showed average precipitation for those destinations, and the latest forecast is slightly more encouraging. We still recommend choosing higher elevation ski areas to pad your odds for snow rather than rain.

NOAA’s next seasonal outlook is scheduled for December 17. Until then, skiers will have to keep watching the shorter-range forecasts and hope the promising signals translate into the kind of winter the West desperately needs.

Watch: Jessie Diggins Explains Why Sparkles Are Her Superpower

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Trail Runner managing editor Abby Levene caught up with cross-country skiing superstar Jessie Diggins in Kona, Hawaii, a few days before the Ironman World Championship.
  • It has been revealed that after retiring from cross-country skiing as the most decorated American of all time, glide off into the sunset Jessie Diggins did not.
  • It has been revealed that diggins, 35, raced the Broken Arrow Triple Crown in June, as has become her annual ritual.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Trail Runner managing editor Abby Levene caught up with cross-country skiing superstar Jessie Diggins in Kona, Hawaii, a few days before the Ironman World Championship. In this exclusive interview, Diggins shares how she battled through a deep low to finish (and win) her first 100-miler, the lessons from cross-country skiing that she’s applying to trail running, and why she always puts on face glitter before a race.

It has been revealed that after retiring from cross-country skiing as the most decorated American of all time, glide off into the sunset Jessie Diggins did not. The Olympic gold medalist earned one last piece of hardware in Milan-Cortina this spring—on bruised ribs no less—hung up the skis, and dove head-first into trail running.

It has been revealed that diggins, 35, raced the Broken Arrow Triple Crown in June, as has become her annual ritual. She then lined up against the world’s best trail runners at Sierre-Zinal in August, won the Superior 100-miler in September, and just last weekend won the (bear with me) Trail Animals Running Club Stone Cat Trail Festival 50-miler in Massachusetts.

Industry observers note that on paper, it’s been an effortless transition into a sport Diggins swears she is just doing for fun. But of course there is so much more to the story once you dig in. I was lucky enough to catch up with Diggins at the epicenter of yet another endurance sport—the Ironman World Championship—in Kona, Hawaii, last month. She’d just come from a snorkeling expedition trying to find a sea turtle. (So far no luck.) Gazing out onto the turquoise waves crashing into shore, we chatted about what she’s learned and loved about trail running so far. That list includes (and is not limited to) how trail running really is a team sport, achieving personal goals is bigger than the results, fueling on a “washing machine” stomach is not easy, and the power of glitter translates from snowy trails to dry ones.

This interview has been edited for clarity. You can also watch some of it above.

Industry observers note that jessie: It was a really cool experience. It was so humbling, but so exciting to tackle a totally different challenge. I was filled with curiosity: What will this feel like? What’s going to happen to my body? What will happen inside my brain? How does this work?

Having a crew and pacers like that is very different from skiing. [In skiing] you are alone on the trail, and people can cheer for you, but you don’t actually have anyone with you on the trail. And so it was just so exciting I got to do it with a team. That was really big for me. I’m a very team-oriented person, and I would get so excited to come into the aid station and see the crew and to get to have a pacer with me. Even when I was falling apart and couldn’t even  talk—I was at a really low point—it was just like, ‘I’m here with my team and I’m pushing my limits and I’m seeing what’s possible for me.’ And that’s so exciting.

I would just tell myself ‘every step you take is a step you don’t have to take again.’ So I was just like, ‘I’m doing it. I’m slowly working towards that finish line, step by step.’ It was so funny because even when I was deeply uncomfortable, I never actually thought about quitting, which I thought I would. It was more just like I’m so uncomfortable, but I know I can if I just keep moving. Even if I’m slowing down, even if I’m not even able to run, I have to just power hike this section. I’m still moving towards my goal. I’m in the process of getting there, and that’s exciting in and of itself.

I kind of wanted to set up a charcuterie board of the trail world and try different things because they were all so different, right? Broken Arrow is a huge festival and it was a multi-day thing, so oh my gosh, what is day three gonna feel like? Can I even run downhill on day three?

And then Sierre-Zinal is so historic, and it was such a cool course. It was beautiful, and it was like experiencing a very classic “short” trail race, right? I was like, ‘this is not short.’ It took me 3 hours, but it was so cool to experience.

In a recent development, and then going into the 100 miler, it was different and more of a backyard format. Or not a backyard in terms of the laps, but like there was no award ceremony. It wasn’t about winning. It was just about doing it, and I love that. That is so aligned with how I feel about racing. It’s like, ‘No, we don’t really care who wins. We just want everyone to challenge themselves and hopefully make their goal of crossing the finish line.’ And that was so cool for me.

And so getting to be a part of each of these events, I got to experience so many different angles of the trail world and meet so many people. And for me, that was a substantial thing, too: feeling the sense of community that was around every single race and making new friends and trying something new. That was very cool.

No, I definitely am excited to do more. I don’t know what that’s gonna look like yet, but I feel like just getting to be involved in this world is so cool and so exciting. So, I’m sort of now in the phase of like, ‘OK, I feel like I’m bouncing back with 100. Like, my body’s coming back, and now I can start dreaming and scheming and brainstorming, like what else do I want to do? What else is out there? What excites me? What feels like the appropriate challenge for this phase of my life?’ Yeah, I’m trying to figure it all out.

I think the biggest thing was in training, like listening to my body. So I stopped wearing a heart rate monitor like five or six years ago, and it was really about being in tune and listening to my body and figuring out where I can push. What does it feel like when I’m riding that line of level three, and what are the signals in my body when I’ve gone over that line and I need to pull it back?

Industry observers note that and so really trying to deeply understand how I feel, and I feel like that’s helped me steer away from injuries too, because I’m not relying on metrics. I want to feel how my body feels and respond to that and act on those feelings.I think that’s something I’m taking with me because I’m well aware now that running can really beat you up in a different way. Even listening to my body and learning how much can I eat while I’m running because your stomach is a washing machine and that does not happen in cross-country skiing.

Recent findings suggest that I think it was really exciting in my final years of cross-country skiing, learning more about high-carb fueling and having all these great products come on board. Because in a ski race, let’s say a 50-kilometer race, you come through a feed zone, but you have gloves and your hands are in poles, so you are not like ripping open a gel. You’ll end up stabbing yourself in the face. And so what you do is you tuck your poles under your armpits and you grab the feed bottle, which is usually an actual baby bottle with the lid taken off, from a coach who cannot run with you, they have to just stand there and hold it by the rim. So you grab it while you are gliding quite quickly. You down it so you get like a few good sips, and then you have to chuck the bottle on the side and keep moving. And so having really high carb drink mixes where you can, if you only can get a few mouthfuls, you need them to count, and so having these was huge. Because before it’d be like, ‘I guess we’ll boil down Coke to de-fizz it, and that’s what you can have.’ But it  just wasn’t high carb enough, and the electrolyte balance might not have been great.

Now there’s so many options, and that really changed the way I could race. And so now, in trail racing, there’s all these different gels. You can find the one that works for you. There’s all these different mixes. You can find the amount of salt that works for you. That’s been really cool. Being able to tailor it. I feel like 15 years ago, there weren’t that many options. Now having more options is power.

I do get scared. It’s funny. I just saw on the elevator this morning a woman was wearing glitter, and I was like, ‘Yes!’ That was my whole thing through my ski career. And it came out of being scared and being nervous. And I feel like people don’t always know that that’s the origin. But I would get so nervous for races, and a little bit of nerves is great. It means you care. If you’re not nervous for a race, it’s sort of like, ‘Why am I doing this?’ You know, then it’s time to maybe examine, do I really care about what I’m doing?

According to recent reports, at the end of the day, yes, there’s a lot of pressure. There can be expectations. There can be a lot of lights. A lot of people are watching you, but you get to do this. You get to challenge yourself and see what’s possible. And that, in and of itself, is such an amazing opportunity.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Southern Illinois school teacher Darin Hicks grew up in a hunting family, but he didn’t start hunting deer himself until just a few years ago. As his interest in deer hunting grew, he took special notice of any significant bucks he spotted during his daily drives to and from school as a science teacher.

“I started seeing a large buck, but never in the day [at first],” the 40-year-old Illinois native tells Outdoor Life. “We don’t use trail cameras. But I got plenty of [phone] photos the last couple years of a really good buck — but only a few photos during the day.”.

Hicks was mentoring his 9-year-old daughter, Josie, who wanted her first deer to be a buck.

“I had her out in youth season, and she could have taken a lot of does but wanted a buck. One evening we saw a buck, but it was too dark [even though it was still legal light] and Josie didn’t want to shoot in that poor light.”.

Hicks thinks the buck that he and his daughter spotted that evening during the youth season may have been the giant buck he arrowed weeks later.

According to recent reports, on Nov. 14 he hung a ladder stand near a wooded thicket full of rubs, scrapes, and plenty of trails. He set the stand for his dad, 77, to hunt during the upcoming Illinois gun opener on Nov. 20.

But that Saturday night Hicks’ wife, Katie, asked her husband if he wanted to bowhunt the stand the next day, before his father got in it the following week.

Hicks stated there wasn’t much time that next morning on Sunday before they left for church. Katie said he had a good two hours to hunt from dawn until leaving for church with his family.

According to recent reports, she had a good point, Hicks decided, and climbed into the stand the following morning of Nov. 15.

According to recent reports, he sat for about an hour and spotted a doe with twin fawns at 150 yards. Suddenly the doe with young spooked and out stepped the giant buck Hicks had seen from afar for the last two years.

“I was shaking, found my grunt call and blew it once,” he states. “He turned and started walking toward me and my heart was pounding overtime.”.

The buck came steadily closer while Hicks readied for a shot — the first time he would ever draw his bow on a whitetail.

In a recent development, “He walked toward me, stopped, and looked up at me at 15 yards, then he turned to head away,” Hicks notes. “He started through some brush quartering away at 35 yards and I drew, released, and I heard a loud smack.”.

According to recent reports, the buck collapsed in his tracks. Hicks’ arrow had hit a bit high, but his 2-blade mechanical struck the spine and the buck didn’t get up.

Hicks managed to wrestle the nontypical out of the woods and, field-dressed, it weighed 187 pounds. His taxidermist aged the buck at 5 1/2 years, with a gross green score of 226 1/8 inches.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Two unbelievable sights in one spot: a dog trapped in a deep fissure in the ground, and a crew lowering a man into that fissure to save her.
  • This scene unfolded in southern Idaho on Nov.
  • It has been revealed that “1,200 miles from home hunting a new bird,” wrote Kyle Stokke in an Instagram post on Nov.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Two unbelievable sights in one spot: a dog trapped in a deep fissure in the ground, and a crew lowering a man into that fissure to save her.

This scene unfolded in southern Idaho on Nov. 8. After a traveling bird hunter’s pointer fell some 60-feet into a basalt crack while hunting wild birds, he had to call in a professional rescue team for help.

It has been revealed that “1,200 miles from home hunting a new bird,” wrote Kyle Stokke in an Instagram post on Nov. 12. “[I] was naively unaware of the unique dangers in these new environments.”.

A post shared by Kyle Stokke (@kyle.stokke).

Stokke posted a four-minute rescue video last week. Earlier posts show him hunting upland birds with two dogs: a German shorthaired pointer and a Labrador retriever. The trio camped while traveling 1,200 miles cross-country from the Midwest to Idaho. Trouble started when the GSP, Esther, fell into a deep fissure.

It has been revealed that “Good gracious!” an unseen rescuer says in the video. “She is down there a freaking long ways.”.

Esther fell at least 60 feet. The fissure went deeper than that, but she landed on a ledge above the true bottom. In the video, you can hear her whines echo up the crack as Stokke, filming from above, reassures her.

“It’s okay Esther,” he indicates. “You’re a good girl.”.

Sources indicate that magic Valley Paramedics has a dedicated unit called the Special Operations Rescue Team. SORT is a highly trained, 20-person volunteer crew specializing in low- and high-angle rope rescues.

Industry observers note that “The biggest challenge was finding exactly where she was,” Chad Smith, SORT team leader, tells Outdoor Life. “Sound travels differently in the canyon. You could hear her so she seemed close, but she wasn’t. How sound travels in there is really deceiving. It threw us off a little bit.”.

SORT averages 20 rescues a year in Twin Falls and Jerome counties. In Smith’s 15 years with SORT, the team has rescued four dogs from fissures, including another bird dog stuck in a similar crack during a previous hunting season. Esther’s rescue happened to fall on the first day of SORT’s semiannual, three-day training exercises.

Sources indicate that “The rescue truck is pulled out and everyone is practicing anchors when the supervisor asks if we want to rescue a dog,” reads a post by the organization. “Who can say no to a dog? Training shifts gears real quick.”.

The video shows the team straddling a 2-foot-wide black void hidden in flat sagebrush country.

Industry observers note that “Wow! I can see her,” notes someone offscreen as one rescuer, Trevor Churchman, is slowly lowered into the tight divide on a harness, ropes, and straps rigged to a large tripod set over the opening.

It has been revealed that “Tell Kyle she’s doing good,” says Churchman. “She’s walking around and she’s wagging her tail.”.

A few minutes later, both man and dog are hoisted out of the crack, and Esther, apparently unharmed, is handed to Stokke. He’s visibly shaking in the video and sounds emotional, but manages a “thank you” for the crew and a “whoa” to keep Esther steady, since everyone is standing near the edge.

“Okay guys, remember there’s an edge there,” a rescuer says. “We don’t have a lot of you guys on ropes.”.

Industry observers note that the two-hour rescue took place in terrain shaped by prehistoric volcanic activity. Tunnels, lava tubes, cliffs, caves, and crevices run through much of the area’s undeveloped public land. (If that’s hard to picture, think of the better-known volcanic landscape at Craters of the Moon National Monument and Preserve, 90 miles north of Twin Falls.).

Water filters through the porous basalt rock formations, creating seeps, springs, and waterfalls that feed the Snake River, which has carved a deep canyon that’s home to the dramatic spray of Shoshone Falls.

Recent findings suggest that “When hiking around the canyon, cracks in the rock can be quite deep,” the rescue team warns. “This one was deeper than 45 feet. We could not see the bottom, and they can fill with tumbleweeds making them look like level ground. So watch your step.”.

Industry observers note that it’s rough, remote country that attracts extreme adventurers like BASE jumpers. And it can surprise even experienced bird hunters, such as Stokke, who assume they’re hunting in relatively flat country.

#114380. Simms Rip Line PRO Review: We Tested This Heavy-Duty Fishing Rain Gear in Downpours and High Winds

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1576 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Outdoorlife ↗ Open Full Page

Simms Rip Line PRO Review: We Tested This Heavy-Duty Fishing Rain Gear in Downpours and High Winds

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1576 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs.
  • Simms has long been an industry staple for fishing apparel, most notably waders and outerwear.
  • Recent findings suggest that enter Simms’ new Rip Line Pro series of rain gear, the tech giant’s first attempt at a truly hardcore jacket and bibs designed specifically for watermen.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›.

Simms has long been an industry staple for fishing apparel, most notably waders and outerwear. I’ve tested and reviewed many Simms products, including its Challenger lineup of rain gear. While that gear has always performed well, its target market is clear: dedicated recreational anglers. I’ve never bothered to test how Simms outerwear handles the trials and tribulations of everyday use by commercial deckhands or saltwater captains because, frankly, why would I? That’s not the audience it’s intended for, and I wouldn’t expect rain gear designed for landlocked fly anglers to hold up for someone used to hauling crab traps in salt spray and freezing rain all day.

Recent findings suggest that enter Simms’ new Rip Line Pro series of rain gear, the tech giant’s first attempt at a truly hardcore jacket and bibs designed specifically for watermen. The Rip Line Pro series forgoes much of the aesthetic and, shall we say, fanciness of Simms’ standard recreation-oriented rain gear in favor of pure, rugged functionality. From the moment you see the Rip Line Pro jacket and bibs, it’s clear they aren’t meant for a hike down to your favorite blue-ribbon trout stream. Pick them up and feel them in hand, and that point is driven home. This is not casual rain gear, and it doesn’t sacrifice performance for looks. It’s designed for abuse of the highest order, the kind dished out by Mother Nature on the open sea.

So, how does it handle that? The look and feel right out of the box make a promise, but does the Rip Line Pro series deliver? To find out, I spent a few weeks putting this gear through the wringer in one of the best testing grounds I could think of: the Chesapeake Bay in late fall and early winter. Read on to see how the Rip Line Pro performed.

When it comes to testing gear, sometimes the timing doesn’t line up. Given the monthslong drought in the Mid-Atlantic leading up to my test, I was worried that might be the case here. As it turned out, that worry was misplaced. Exactly one day after the Rip Line Pro gear arrived, the forecast called for an epic deluge paired with extreme wind and storms. It was the perfect blend of miserable fishing conditions for testing rain gear. Lucky me.

The forecast proved accurate, and the weather was extreme, almost to a fault. I spent the first few hours of the morning sheltering from lightning under a dockhouse on the water. The Rip Line Pro gear will protect you from a lot, but I don’t think “lightning strike” is on the list. Thankfully, the electrical portion of the storm passed, and I had the rest of the day to fish in a constant downpour and gusting wind.

After a few hours of fishing from a kayak in the rain and getting sprayed with salt water, the first thing I checked was the areas where most rain gear performs worst: the wrists, neck, and ankles. These are typically the hardest spots to protect because they offer a direct path for water to get beneath the rain gear, and they still need to allow some comfort and range of motion. The Rip Line Pro did an outstanding job of keeping moisture out of all three. The wrists and forearms were the most impressive. They feature an extended 1-millimeter neoprene cuff beneath the outer layer that lets this jacket perform almost like a full dry top. Not only does it keep rain out, but the neoprene cuff creates a seal that kept water from flowing down the sleeve even when my arm was fully submerged. I was equally impressed by the neck. While it doesn’t have the full neoprene seal of the sleeves, the hood design and zipper-and-Velcro combination created an impressively form-fitting seal that kept water from dripping down my back or chest. Finally, the ankle cuffs on the bibs did an excellent job of keeping spray and rainwater away from my feet. I was wearing ankle-height deck boots, and the leg cuffs paired perfectly with them to create an angled seal where no water could enter.

According to recent reports, next, I inspected the storage, namely the various dry pockets on both the jacket and bibs. Each has a well-designed, easily accessible exterior pocket sealed by a watertight zipper and tucked beneath a Velcro storm flap for extra protection. Exterior pockets on rain gear are always a gamble, but accessible waterproof storage is important. The pockets on the Rip Line Pro jacket and bibs performed exceptionally well, even after I opened and closed them many times throughout the day to reach various items. Nothing seeped through the pockets to the interior of the suit, and the pockets kept everything inside them dry and functional.

Dry storage and adjustable cuffs matter, but ultimately the most important job of rain gear is keeping you dry all day long. While I was impressed with how well the Rip Line Pro kept water out of various areas throughout the day, the real test would be how wet and cold I got after fishing in rain and wind for upward of 12 hours.

Industry observers note that the answer? Not very. For me, the most impressive part of this gear is the overall protection it offered from the elements. After we returned to the boat ramp and loaded our gear, it was time to strip off the rain suit and inspect the damage. No matter how dry you think you are, a bit of unforeseen moisture usually gets through any rain gear after a long day. Apart from a few wet spots where my shirt had been exposed during the day, I was basically bone-dry. The jacket and bibs also did a great job of blocking wind chill. I had underestimated how well that was working during the day, but looking back, I realized how much the gear kept the wind from affecting my comfort. Not that I needed confirmation, but watching my fishing partners shiver miserably and wring out sopping undershirts provided a sense of warm relief, both physically and emotionally.

Protection from the elements, plain and simple. I’ve worn many bibs and rain jackets over the years, some designed for comfort and others for function. The Rip Line Pro does the best job I’ve found of marrying the two, though function is still clearly the priority.

Once you’re fully suited up, this rain gear makes you feel practically invincible, protected by an impenetrable shell of armor. I’m not saying it’s bulletproof, but I could feel an unrealistic sense of confidence building while I wore it. The materials not only kept me bone-dry through a full day of torrential rain but also provided exceptional wind protection during gusts upward of 30 knots. When it comes to protection from extreme water and wind, the Rip Line Pro series is as good as it gets.

With extreme weather protection as the focus, it’s easy to understand why some other features take a back seat. That said, there are still a few areas I’d like to see Simms improve.

The most noticeable is the lack of mobility. The four-layer construction and fully waterproof material make this gear weatherproof, but they also make it rather cumbersome. Simms added articulation points and adjustable areas where possible, but there’s still room for improvement. At times, I felt a bit like a piece of vacuum-sealed meat, or a video game character bolted into a mech suit. Yes, I felt invincible, but I also had a harder time than I care to admit squatting to grab a sandwich from the cooler.

Insulation is another area that could be better. The Rip Line Pro gear does an incredible job of protecting you from water and wind, but it doesn’t have much interior insulation for true winter use. That’s easy to offset by layering proper cold-weather clothing underneath, but I could see a built-in cold-weather liner helping. Perhaps Simms will release a “winter” edition of the Rip Line Pro in the future with a wool liner or something similar.

The Rip Line Pro series of rain gear is not for everyone. In fact, I would say the target market for this gear is fairly narrow. Most casual anglers and outdoor enthusiasts can get by with less extreme, less expensive rain gear and never have an problem. While this gear is fantastic at keeping you dry, I could see it being overkill for an after-work outing during a light summer shower.

However, what the Rip Line Pro series is designed to do, it does extremely well, and the people who need this type of gear will appreciate it. The Rip Line Pro series is built for serious anglers and people who spend as much time on the water as on dry land. As with any gear in the fishing space, the more purpose-built something becomes, the less universal appeal it tends to have. That mentioned, if you fish as much as I do, serious rain gear becomes less a matter of convenience and more a matter of necessity. The Rip Line Pro jacket and bibs offer the type of performance and functionality I value, and I’m sure many other anglers, deckhands, and charter captains who try them will agree.

My blueprint was to knock on doors asking for permission to hunt and camp on a landowner’s property. While this sort of adventure — relying on permission for an entire hunt in unknown territory — occurs less frequently than it did years ago, I was pleased to discover that it is still possible.

Once I secured permission, the next challenge would be getting within bow range of a deer.

It has been revealed that over the course of three days in mostly wide-open country, I found myself moving through the perfect puzzle-solving experience that deer hunters are so fond of: locating deer, then figuring out how to hunt them. On the first day, I found deer. On the second day, I nearly pulled the trigger on a shooter buck. And on the third day, I sent an arrow at the biggest buck I’d ever shot.

#114377. Tech Report: Historic Drought Looms Over Arkansas Duck Opener. What Few Ducks Show Up Face Heavy Pressure

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1330 w)

Tech Report: Historic Drought Looms Over Arkansas Duck Opener. What Few Ducks Show Up Face Heavy Pressure

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1330 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, if you asked any serious waterfowl hunter to name their dream duck-hunting destinations, Arkansas would be at the top of nearly every list.
  • Yet in 2026, Arkansas’ waterfowl season is suddenly looking bleak.
  • For 14 months Arkansas has been without any serious rainfall, leaving rich croplands and, more importantly for ducks, wetlands, drier than they’ve been in decades.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, if you asked any serious waterfowl hunter to name their dream duck-hunting destinations, Arkansas would be at the top of nearly every list. Its classic flooded hardwoods and bayous along with the state’s rich rice and grain fields, lure massive flights of puddle ducks and geese to its hallowed waters every year. This has made Arkansas stand out above other southern states as the beating heart of the Mississippi Flyway.

Yet in 2026, Arkansas’ waterfowl season is suddenly looking bleak. A historic drought has many duck hunters worried ahead of the Nov. 21 opener, as the serious lack of water could bring duck hunting to a standstill. Duck hunters on both public and private land may have some serious decisions to make to safeguard ducks and future duck seasons.

For 14 months Arkansas has been without any serious rainfall, leaving rich croplands and, more importantly for ducks, wetlands, drier than they’ve been in decades. Every corner of the state is under a severe drought status, with some areas being more than 20 inches behind in cumulative rainfall totals.

To put the drought in perspective, this is slated to be the state’s third-driest October through January since record keeping began in 1895.

This leaves the Arkansas Game and Fish Commission with very little water to spare, to the point where the agency expects it will only be able to flood around 40 of its more than 70 moist-soil public-land hunting units.

“In my 50 years of duck hunting in Arkansas, I don’t remember it ever being as dry as this,” notes Brent Birch, founder of Arkansas’ Greenhead magazine. “It’s been this way all summer and well into the fall. And even with the prospects of a Super El Niño, we have nothing the forecast that says it’s going to resolve anytime soon.”.

Without an incredible amount of rainfall in a short amount of time, Birch and other waterfowlers around the state are worried not only about not having places to hunt, but that the ducks may not even show up.

“So far, we are seeing a few groups of gadwalls, pintails, and other early migrating ducks but not in anything close to their usual numbers,” Birch says. “And when it comes to incoming mallards, you can pretty much forget it. It’s just too dry for them. The fact is the closer it gets to 2027 under these conditions, the worse the entire duck season is going to be. And if we don’t start getting some wet weather soon to push ducks down here, we’re looking at a poor outlook for the entire season.”.

The reason that Arkansas waterfowl hunting is so good is that it lies at the north end of the historic feeding grounds for ducks and geese in the Mississippi Flyway. Once the cold sets in around their spring and summer breeding grounds in Canada, the birds come south to binge on Arkansas’ rich wetlands throughout the winter. However, with the current drought, the fear is that the incoming ducks will be forced to fly elsewhere.

According to recent reports, “Ducks coming south to Arkansas aren’t like ducks in northern states,” indicates Ducks Unlimited Arkansas regional biologist Jake Spears, who lives in Jonesboro. “Northern birds are more apt to feed in dry fields so long as they have a body of water to roost on nearby. However, in the Southern U.S., they stop feeding in fields and primarily feed in water. They look for things like water plants and waste grains in flooded fields, which Arkansas currently just doesn’t have.”.

Spears worries that many ducks are going to fly to Arkansas and then be forced to turn northward again or keep driving south.

“The ducks need food so they may go to Louisiana, or Kansas, or Missouri — wherever they can find that food source,” says Spears. “Which is going to leave both public-land duck hunters and even most hunting clubs just completely out of luck.”.

Private-land duck-hunting clubs are a popular option for many Arkansas hunters and visiting nonresidents, as even during droughts, most clubs can pump water to create duck habitat and attract birds. The 2026 drought has been so bad, however, that many clubs won’t even have the water to pump.

Recent findings suggest that this is especially troubling to some public-land waterfowl hunters, who worry that the private hunting clubs that can still pump water may end up attracting what few ducks do make it to Arkansas. This could result in a season that benefits the haves over the have-nots.

In a recent development, “I think hunting clubs are the only thing that’s going to make Arkansas appealing for ducks right now,” Spears states. “Most of the smaller rivers, sloughs, and backwaters we have on public land can be walked across in flip-flops right now. So the clubs that have the option to flood fields and create habitat are where the birds are going to be. But with the water table so low, clubs with the ability to pump will be few and far between, so any ducks that do show up during the season are going to have to be babied quite a bit.”.

The fact is that if the drought continues in Arkansas, duck hunters on both public and private land alike are going to have to weigh their priorities. Drought conditions are going to be tough on ducks that migrate through Arkansas, and hunting pressure will make surviving the migration harder even for birds that aren’t killed.

This leaves duck hunters with a choice to make.

It has been revealed that “It’s going to come down to responsible management on all sides because if we want to maintain the ducks we have, we have to be careful with them,” Birch notes. “There are several components to management. It’s not just hunting and the noise of guns, we must be careful disturbing the ducks in any capacity. Your vehicle is an concern because you’re going to bump ducks going in and out of your hunting area, and you’re going to have to be real careful with how many days you hunt and how many hours you hunt in a day, because you’re going to have to let the birds rest.”.

With Arkansas’ duck season lasting a total of 51 days with two relatively short splits, hunters looking to limit out consistently are going to be putting serious pressure on what will already be a limited resource.

So instead of hunting hard, both Birch and Spears recommend self-imposed bag limits and time on the water so that the resource can continue to both be conserved and shared.

“My suggestion to any duck hunter in Arkansas is that if you have ducks on your property, take care of them,” notes Spears. “With the limited resources, they aren’t going to be able to handle a lot of pressure. You’re going to have to limit how much you hunt and how many birds you shoot, and not be afraid to cut your hunt short. Get a few birds and then leave so the ducks can get back to the water to feed.”.

Industry observers note that read Next: Has Hot Cropping Ruined Duck Hunting? Here’s What the Data and Biologists Say About How Flooded Corn Affects Waterfowl Migration.

According to recent reports, while there is hope that conditions will change, the fact is that the whole of Arkansas’ 2026 duck season may be a nonstarter for many hunters. That short-term pain, however, could help future duck seasons look a little brighter. Spears and Birch are hopeful for a future where water and the waterfowl will eventually return, filling the skies and waterways like flowing veins and once again making Arkansas the beating heart of the Mississippi Flyway itself.

“We need to be good stewards of the resource,” urges Spears. “Hunters should do everything they can to keep [ducks] around and not shoot them off what water we do have.”.

#114375. Latest Update: Old-School Whitetail Wisdom for Filling Your Tag After Opening Day

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 16m • 📚 Deep Dive (3256 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outdoorlife ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Old-School Whitetail Wisdom for Filling Your Tag After Opening Day

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3256 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that these days, a buck can’t grow to trophy proportions on hard-hunted public lands by folding up under the pressure exerted by the opening-day crush of hunters.
  • Recent findings suggest that some substantial bucks live in locations that allow them to avoid the opening weekend crowd by slipping into the sanctuary offered by state parks, game refuges or private posted land.
  • But the whitetail is a homebody at heart, and he is most comfortable on his loosely defined home turf.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that these days, a buck can’t grow to trophy proportions on hard-hunted public lands by folding up under the pressure exerted by the opening-day crush of hunters. A whitetail lives the 3½ years necessary to grow a bragging set of antlers by learning to cope with the annual influx of hunters during the season’s first days. Every opening day that the buck survives increases his chance of surviving the ensuing openers, as well.

Recent findings suggest that some substantial bucks live in locations that allow them to avoid the opening weekend crowd by slipping into the sanctuary offered by state parks, game refuges or private posted land. Others crawl into the most inaccessible and gosh-awful cover their “territory” has to offer — the kind of place hunters walk around, rather than through — and stay there until the crowds leave. And on more than one occasion, I have found a bruiser buck in a tiny, secluded patch of isolated cover — the kind of place most hunters never think to look in.

But the whitetail is a homebody at heart, and he is most comfortable on his loosely defined home turf. You can bet that once the steady crack of opening day rifles slackens to only an occasional pop, those significant bucks will be right back to business as usual. And that is the precise reason why your best chance for bagging a wall-hanger occurs after the opening day madness has subsided.

Where you begin your search for that after-the-opener buck hinges upon one factor: the rut. Many states strategy their firearms seasons to coincide with the rut, offering their hunters every opportunity to harvest the surplus bucks. Other states, bound in tradition, open the season after the main rut has ended. If you are planning to travel out of your home state to hunt whitetails, it makes sense to hunt a state where the season coincides with the rut, all other criteria being equal.

Recent findings suggest that A mature whitetail buck is a different character during the rut than he is after it. A buck’s sole purpose at that time is to procreate, and this he does with obvious enthusiasm and the stamina of a teenager. There are stories abounding in every deer camp in the country of the crazy antics performed by bucks under the spell of the “rutting moon,” such as lovesick bucks strolling across open fields in broad daylight. Others tell tales of bucks putting their noses to does’ tracks and following those tracks, even after being shot at and missed several times. Rut-crazed bucks, while under the influence of a powerful rush of hormones, have even been known to either pick fights with or attempt to mate with assorted farm livestock.

In a recent development, so rampant are the stories that I’m afraid there exists a whole contingent of deer hunters laboring under the false assumption that all a hunter needs do to down one of these crazy buggers is to walk into the woods, lean up against a stump and wait for one of the poor, sex-addled dummies to saunter on by. Although such tactics work just often enough to keep the myth perpetuated, plenty of hunters have been sitting against stumps for more unsuccessful years than they will probably admit, and they’re still waiting for a buck to wander by.

Recent findings suggest that hunting whitetails during the rut and after the opening weekend of the season isn’t easy. You must employ all of the skill and woods savvy you have. Any breaks you receive because of a buck’s overactive glands should be considered a bonus.

Sources indicate that after the opener, I refine my hunting strategy for significant bucks by determining what stage the rut is in. This is vital because the stage of the rut will determine where I concentrate most of my midweek hunting efforts.

According to recent reports, the whitetail buck is ready to breed long before the first doe enters estrus. During this period, the buck runs off excess energy by beating up saplings, sparring with bushes and, on occasion, duking it out with other bucks. In the process of making rubs on bushes and trees, the buck deposits scents that tell the rest of the whitetail community who was there.

Scrapes begin to show up in increasing numbers as the level of testosterone builds in the buck’s system. The buck paws out scrapes and leaves his scent both in the bare earth of the scrapes and on overhanging branches above the scrapes. Again, this is a means of communicating with other whitetails. The message to does is that the buck is now standing at stud, and it tells other bucks that they had best move along if they know what’s good for them.

It has been revealed that A buck will paw out most of his scrapes in areas where they are most likely to be seen or smelled by does. Openings in woods, old logging roads and the edges of woodlots are common places to encounter scrapes. A buck may make a dozen or more scrapes, and he’ll check some of them daily, making sure they are free of debris and liberally doused with musk/urine. These are the scrapes to hunt over.

However, once the does begin cycling into heat, the dominant bucks that handle the bulk of the breeding chores are often so busy accompanying, tracking and servicing does that they neither have the time nor the need to freshen their scrapes. But if you find a string of scrapes that have not been freshened for several days, it doesn’t necessarily mean that the rut is over or that the buck that made the scrapes is hanging from someone else’s game pole. It may mean that the buck is out doing his job.

In a recent development, the best way to determine what stage the rut is in is to spend a day or two in the woods prior to the hunt. If fresh scrapes abound, you will be hunting the pre-coital period, and a stand near a scrape line is going to be hard to beat. If, on the other hand, you find that more than half of the scrapes are old and abandoned, it’s a good bet that the massive bucks are out taking care of the does, while the lesser bucks are still hanging around their scrapes, waiting.

If you just don’t have time to get into the woods prior to the season, you can get a good idea about the stage of the rut by speaking with area game managers, milk haulers, rural school bus drivers, postal carriers, loggers, trappers, farmers, grouse hunters, bowhunters or others who spend most of their time in deer country. If the bucks are chasing the does, chances are these people will have observed some of the activity.

Why all of the fuss over determining what stage the rut is in? Because it makes a massive difference when you have to decide how you want to hunt after the opening weekend of the season.

Recent findings suggest that when the season begins, if the actual breeding season has not yet begun but bucks are busy pawing out upcoming scrapes and freshening old ones, chances are the bucks will curtail this activity during the high-pressure days at the beginning of the season, resuming their rounds once the hunters thin out. I like to have at least a half-dozen scrape lines pinpointed prior to the opener, and I check them after the opening weekend for any sign of activity. I then concentrate my hunting efforts near the “hottest” scrapes.

If your pre-season scouting and snooping indicates that the actual breeding season is in progress, then hunting over scrapes may not be your best option for tagging a really good buck. Remember, it is often the massive, dominant bucks in the area that handle the bulk of the breeding chores. Even in an area with an excellent buck-to-doe ratio, a breeding buck can be kept so busy that he has little time or need to tend his scrapes. Often, a buck will spend 24 hours with the same doe, breeding her several times before her cycle ends. At this time, it is the doe, not the buck, that determines where the pair will travel. Though I would not totally rule out hunting in the vicinity of inactive scrapes at this stage of the rut, there are other options that I’ve found give me a better chance at tagging a big buck.

One of my favorite methods during this period is to concentrate my hunting efforts in areas where I have encountered good numbers of does in the past. Does and fawns tend to hang around together, and they routinely congregate in specific areas, often bedding as a loosely knit group in a favorite swale or sunny hillside. I can’t direct you to these “ladies-only bedrooms,” but I’ll bet there is such a place in the chunk of woods you hunt.

According to recent reports, you can locate these places that hold special favor with the does by simply noting those areas where you encounter the most doe activity. After a few years of hunting the same ground, a familiar pattern becomes apparent.

Industry observers note that on several occasions, I have located a hotbed of doe activity by simply listening to other hunters. When you hear a hunter complain that he sat on his stand and saw 15 does but not a single buck, find out where he was sitting. You can bet that when the time is right, there will be a buck or two sniffing around the vicinity.

A dominant buck ranges well out of his home area during the actual breeding season. I don’t think he goes out of his way looking for does so much as he is drawn out of the territory when following the tracks of a doe that has visited his scrapes or just wandered through the area. A buck engaged in this activity moves with a single-minded purpose, shuffling along, nose to the ground, seldom looking up, intent upon finding the maker of the tracks he is following. I once missed a buck that trailed a doe past my tree stand in this manner, my arrow slicing harmlessly over the buck’s back only to skitter noisily through the carpet of dry oak leaves a few yards beyond. The buck lifted his head and looked in the direction of the commotion. Apparently satisfied that whatever had made the racket was not what he was looking for, he then ambled on his way while I frantically fumbled around trying to nock another arrow.

Sources indicate that when a buck finally tracks down a doe, as often as not, she will then lead the buck on a little chase that, in all likelihood, will take the buck still farther from his home base. By the time the buck actually mates with the doe, he may be miles from his original starting point. On the way back to his core area, it is not unlikely that the buck will cut the track of another “hot” doe and repeat the scenario.

It has been revealed that all of this rambling makes it impossible to pattern a buck during the height of the breeding season, prompting many knowledgeable whitetail hunters to claim that taking a good buck during the peak of the rut is mostly a matter of luck. I disagree.

Hunting near a known “doe hangout” can help. And you can stack the deck in your favor even more by hunting a funnel area near a concentration of does. A funnel is simply any natural or man-made feature of the terrain that restricts the movement of deer. An hourglass-shaped section of woods is the classic funnel. Deer moving from one wide portion of the hourglass to the other must pass through the narrow waist. In farm country, the funnel may be a brushy fenceline connecting two woodlots. In the rugged country of the West, where whitetails are becoming increasingly common, a jutting jaw of sheer rimrock can force whitetails into a confined passage. Funnels work well because even though a buck with a snootful of “hot” doe scent wouldn’t care if he was standing in the middle of Madison Avenue, the does do not lose their heads. Does will stick to cover when on the move, even when there is a grunting, panting Romeo dogging their every move.

In many whitetail states, hunters are left with no choice but to hunt well after the main rutting period is over. At first, hunting after the opening weekend under these circumstances appears to be a futile endeavor. Without the promise of the rut to keep the bucks on the move, and with the absence of hunters to jar deer loose, what chance does the midweek hunter have of scoring on a decent buck? He has a pretty good one, I would say.

Industry observers note that first, although the bulk of the breeding chores are completed in about a two-week period, there is still some activity after the main rut is over. Does that were not impregnated will cycle back into heat 28 days after their first estrus cycle ends. In some states, this is just about the time the rifle season rolls around. In addition, in some of the best whitetail areas, it is not uncommon for female fawns of the year to breed. This often applies to as many as 40 percent of them. Frequently, these young breeders experience their first estrus cycle later than older does. So, don’t strike out the possibility of the rut working in your favor even though the peak has passed. In that part of Minnesota where I live, the bulk of the breeding is completed by mid-November, yet each year, I find active scrapes late into November and even December. Last season, during an especially mild December, I found a pair of bushel-basket-size recently freshened scrapes while hunting grouse on Newly introduced Year’s Eve day. If you can find these “late scrapes,” concentrate your hunting efforts near them.

According to recent reports, but even if you fail to find any of these scrapes later in the year, you still stand a good chance of tagging a buck during the middle of the week if you let the after-effects of the rut work in your favor. During the rut, a buck takes little time out to eat. By the end of the breeding season, a buck that began the rut in peak condition can be drawn and thin, actually haggard looking. Some bucks lose up to 20 percent of their body weight during the course of the rut. Across the Northern states and Canada, where winter-kill is an annual problem, the significant, breeding bucks follow the fawns in death each winter simply because they run off all of their reserve fat during the rut and are often unable to replenish it before the onset of winter snows.

Although the largest bucks are often nocturnal in their feeding habits at other times of the year, when the rut is over, dominant bucks cannot afford to limit their foraging to the hours of darkness alone. In order to regain their strength and put on the layer of fat necessary to see them through the winter, they must forage during the day. This gives the after-the-opener hunter the chance he needs to find bucks up and about during shooting hours.

It has been revealed that this need to feed heavily does not necessarily mean that a significant buck will be found sauntering around an alfalfa field at high noon, scarfing down the last frost-tinged greens of the year. It does mean that rather than tucking himself safely away in a thicket long before the morning sun ever peeks over the ridge, a buck will now tend to linger at the feeding grounds longer in the morning. Does and fawns often feed for an hour after sunrise, and now, bucks will begin to do the same. In the evening, when they normally would not begin feeding until complete darkness had fallen, bucks will now arrive at the feeding sites earlier — often in that last precious minute of shooting light.

According to recent reports, even at midday, the major boys will not be content to simply lay in their beds and chew their cuds. I have noticed that once the rut is over, bucks are much more likely to rise from their beds and spend an hour or two at midday — often between 11 a.m. and 2 p.m. — browsing near their bedding sites.

All of this daylight activity is a substantial plus for the after-the-opener hunter who must depend upon natural deer movements, rather than other hunters, to put a buck in front of him. The natural inclination is to hunt from a stand near the feeding area, but this is a mistake when you’re after mature bucks. A big buck is constantly alert, using each of his senses to detect the slightest hint of danger. Never is a buck more alert than when he is feeding during shooting light because he knows he is most vulnerable then. The bucks I have observed feeding during the season have been wound-up tighter than a watch spring and ready to snap at the slightest provocation. One miscue on your part, whether it is movement or scent or whatever, will send him running. I try to avoid known feeding areas, and I concentrate my efforts near the bedding areas.

Hunting near the bedding area means that any shot I take will most often be attempted in good light. That’s crucial for a clean kill. A buck may not arrive back at his bedding area until the sun is an hour high in the morning, and he may leave his bed to begin a dawdling trip to the feeding area in late afternoon. Instead of risking a poor shot at a shadowy form in the gray gloom of dusk or dawn, I take my shot when the light is in my favor.

Industry observers note that also, by concentrating my efforts in the vicinity of the buck’s daytime haunts, I have a better chance of catching him up and about during the midday hours. If I am forced to move into the bedding area and take a stand at mid-morning, I risk detection by the buck. But if I move into my stand in the dark and set up quietly, I double my chances of scoring. If I fail to take the buck as he returns from breakfast, I will be there waiting when he gets up for lunch or dinner.

It has been revealed that but you don’t have to confine yourself to a stand. If conditions allow for quiet stillhunting, I like nothing better than to either prowl the edges of a buck’s daytime haunts or simply tread my way along a ridge littered with the acorns of the white oak, moving only a few yards at a time and stopping often to look, listen and feel. Often after the crowds of opening day are gone from the woods for another year, it is just me and the deer — one-on-one. And that’s the way I like it best.
