How to Clean Overhanging Routes Without Taking the Biggest Swing of Your Life

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 22 min read (4449 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Climbing

⏱️ ~22 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that if you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission.
  • Recent findings suggest that permadraws are incredibly convenient, but sometimes they are not appropriate for an area.
  • In a recent development, so if there are no permadraws, how do you safely clean a steep sport route?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that if you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy.

Recent findings suggest that permadraws are incredibly convenient, but sometimes they are not appropriate for an area. There are a few reasons for this. One is that permadraws are highly visible, turning a natural setting into an outdoor climbing gym. Permadraws also corrode rapidly in marine and coastal environments. Lastly, they are expensive.

In a recent development, so if there are no permadraws, how do you safely clean a steep sport route? Leaving a carabiner is the next easiest solution. But what if you don’t want to do that?

Sources indicate that these nagging questions—as well as recent accidents—have compelled me to put together this long list of options for cleaning your next steep line. I’ve organized these methods into three categories:.

Each method has pros and cons in regards to simplicity, speed, and safety.

Ultimately, no single “best method” exists. Though there is a singular worst method: rappelling. Cleaning steep routes on rappel is a huge hassle for the climber, and bystanders on the ground who inevitably have to assist. Your method of choice will come down to the circumstances of each route and your personal preferences on simplicity, speed, and risk tolerance. Many of these methods are best saved for niche scenarios, or rare “if-then” situations. Still, it is best to be prepared with knowledge and equipment for those odd cleaning scenarios.

Industry observers note that below, I will discuss several methods for cleaning on the way up. I choose this approach if a route has a roof or dangerous swing potential or if, for whatever reason, I’m not ready to clean the route on the way down. Cleaning on the way up can take more time, but it brings safety gains. Methods range from simple to complex. If cleaning on the way down looks like a nuisance, just lower down to the ground and deal with it later (i.e., on the way back up).

Industry observers note that if the route is well within the abilities of someone in your party, toproping to clean is always a good go-to. Never turn down a free toprope, right?

Issues with this method arise when the climbing gets hard enough where the climber might fall on toprope, thus becoming stuck in space. If the climber is unable to get back to the wall and decides to lower, then you may end up needing to re-lead the climb to re-clip the draws/directionals, so someone can attempt cleaning on toprope again. This is a huge pain, but I see it very often. Thankfully, there are many methods that can help you avoid this scenario.

In a recent development, firstly, when someone is toproping to clean, we always say they must promise to get to the top. That way, they won’t leave the rope unclipped from lifesaving directionals. This reminder helps incentivize the climber to “plan falls.” The worst time to fall is immediately after unclipping a bolt, when the swing will be the farthest, potentially leaving the climber stranded. If you think you might fall, it’s best to adequately rest hanging at a bolt before unclipping. Only unclip the bolt once you’re ready to charge to the next one.

What if you get unlucky and fall into space? You can try pulling on the belayer’s end of the rope if it’s within reach. However, this method is usually much less productive on steep topropes than on steep lead climbs. Oftentimes, pulling on the rope will get you nowhere.

If pulling on the rope is getting you nowhere, the next method is boinking. Usually performed on lead, boinking is a strategy a leader can employ after falling into space and becoming unable to reach the rock or a rope. But it does work (albeit sometimes less effectively) on toprope. It’s also tiring and best for short stretches.

The boinking method is simple, but often executed inefficiently. The belayer takes tight on the rope, ideally, and hovers above the ground, or over an edge where they can hang their full body weight. Then, the climber does a pull-up on the climber side of the rope to create a loop of slack. When the climber rapidly releases the slack, the belayer drops. If the belayer is too low to the ground, they will hit the ground, and usually blame the climber.

It has been revealed that for maximum efficiency, the belayer can easily ascend the rope (using an ascender and their Grigri) the same distance that the climber needs to ascend. This obviates the need for timing the boinking/drops and is far more relaxing for both parties. It’s also far more efficient than the belayer jumping to take at the right time.

An alternative to boinking is climbing the leash, as it’s called by highliners. This is the main method highliners use to climb the leash after falling, but also works identically in climbing scenarios when you’re not too far below your clip. If you’re flexible, place your heel above your tie-in knot, then pull on the rope, until you can straighten your leg and reach high for the wall. Once you pull on the wall or a draw, the belayer must rapidly take in all the extra slack.

Have the aforementioned methods become too tiring or inefficient? Or is there too much rope drag or rope stretch in the system for them to be effective? The next method is for the stuck climber to ascend the rope. If I don’t want to do the climbing again, I’ll usually jump straight to this method since I always have an ascender with me at the crag. If it’s just a short section to ascend, a prusik or other autoblock will work fine. But for cleaning a full route, you’ll thank yourself for bringing a proper ascender or at least nano-trax, to the crag (they weigh nothing).

If it is too difficult to pull in and release a draw, you can relocate your ascender above the draw, then clip a PAS/draw into the top carabiner of the draw you wish to clean. Slack the rope from your Grigri to unclip the rope from the draw. If you forgot to move the ascender above the clip, it will get stuck here. Begin ascending again until there is a 90-degree angle between your PAS and tensioned rope. The closer this angle is to 90 degrees, the less muscle required to pull in and unclip the draw. When you unclip the draw from the bolt, it stays attached to your PAS as you go swinging.

Sometimes rope shenanigans can get a bit clunky, especially in roofs. If the bolts are close enough together, you can implement some aid climbing techniques as needed. Sometimes it’s easier to ascend via yarding on bolts, and top-stepping in slings than jugging when it’s really steep. Just do whatever it takes to get up there and reclaim those draws! This can be done in a toprope scenario or a jugging scenario, with a slacked rope, or tensioned.

The biggest error when cleaning steep routes is cleaning on the way down, then taking a dangerous swing low on the route. There are many ways to clean on the way down. We’ll start with the standard scenario, then dive into niche techniques for oddball scenarios.

According to recent reports, many routes have an anchor just below the steep climbing. If this is the case, once you finish cleaning the steep terrain, the first step is to go off belay at that anchor and untie. Then pull the rope from above, re-tie in, and re-lower. When bolting routes, I love adding this type of anchor, not only to provide an easier, shorter version of the route, but also to greatly simplify the process of cleaning lower down the route.

Industry observers note that the most common method for cleaning a steep sport route while lowering is to employ a trolley draw (it goes by many names). This draw connects the belay loop to the belayer’s side of the rope. As you lower, you can pull in on the belayer’s line to clean the draws. Higher up on the route, call for your belayer to hold (stop lowering) when the rope below your trolley draw is nearly level. Lower down on the route, you’ll want to stop sooner, just above the bolt.

There are a few methods for retrieving the draws, but whatever you do, be sure to stop and think before unclipping anything.

The quickest method is to simply grab the wall, pull in (not up) to slack the draw and remove the draw from the bolt. If you can’t grab holds, often you can draw dyno: grab the draw with two hands and thrust in (not up) to momentarily slack the draw to remove it. In either of these cases, it is far more strenuous to remove the rope from the draw since your trolley draw will be yanking you away from the wall when you still have to clean the draw from the bolt. TLDR: If you’re tensioning the trolley, unclip the draw from the bolt.

Industry observers note that if those methods aren’t working, go in direct to the draw you are hoping to retrieve. You can clip your PAS directly to the top carabiner of the draw. If using a draw to go direct, clip an additional draw from the belay loop to the lower carabiner of the draw you wish to clean. It’s best to resist the temptation to relocate the trolley draw into a tether draw. Note that if you remove your trolley draw and do not replace it, you could later unexpectedly fall into space or take a dangerous swing.

In a recent development, once you’ve clipped direct to the draw, you can unclip the rope from the draw you wish to clean, calling slack if needed. Now, unlike other methods, the primary tension is no longer on the trolley, but instead directly on the bolt. Now pull down on the belayer’s rope to assist them in taking. That 90-degree rule applies here, too. Double check that your trolley is in place, assess the swing potential, then remove the draw from the bolt, and take the swing.

The lower you go on the route, the more potential energy—and extra rope—builds up in the system. If the trolley accidentally comes unclipped for any reason, it can be catastrophic. You could swing and hit a rock or a tree. The extra rope could even cause you to hit the ground. For this reason, as I get lower, I’ll often double-up my trolley draw. Why not?

According to recent reports, now let’s imagine we’ve lowered all the way down to the first bolt. As mentioned, the farther we end up from the plumb line, the higher the potential swing risk. Sometimes it is safe to unclip and take the swing. Other times, you might hit trees, rocks, or the ground. If both parties decide the swing is safe, the climber must first unclip the trolley draw before taking the swing. If you forget to unclip the trolley draw, you’ll drag the belayer along the ground as you swing. Very unpleasant!

Industry observers note that if the belayer is firmly anchored you can opt to keep the trolley draw in place to minimize the swing. However, since most sport crags don’t have convenient ground anchors, this option isn’t always possible. Just remember, don’t expect your belayer alone to stop your swing!

In a recent development, if you’re unsure whether a swing is safe, it’s usually best not to risk it. The horizontal distance of a swing is only a small part of understanding the potential impact. A giant King Swing can be perfectly safe, while a seemingly harmless three-foot swing can be devastating. The greater the starting angle of the swing, the more gravitational potential energy the climber has.

Once past the rope’s vertical plumb line (the lowest point of the swing), the climber begins losing speed. However, impact force depends just as much on how abruptly the climber is stopped as it does on their speed. Finally, account for rope stretch, which can increase the swing’s radius and lower the climber’s trajectory. Always make sure your swing won’t put you into the ground or another obstacle!

Sources indicate that even if the swing is all air, there can still be a risk of sharp rock cutting the rope. For this reason, it’s best to avoid big swings if the rope is rubbing rock. Usually, it’s the swing back toward the wall where rope damage is most likely to occur. Ropes cut most commonly from sideways grinding or sliding. If the rope must press rock, I prefer to place the rope where the rock is perpendicular to the rope’s force.

In a recent development, if a swing looks risky, the safest and easiest thing is to leave a draw or a carabiner. In my 20-plus years of sport climbing, I’ve never left a carabiner, but I do love this method because it’s allowed me to collect hundreds of free carabiners over the years, which I repurpose as lower-offs on anchors.

Besides cost, there are additional downsides to leaving gear. It is annoying to clip a bolt that has a bail carabiner. Numerous reported accidents exist wherein a climber falls after clipping a draw to the hanger over an existing carabiner, causing the draw’s carabiner to break. For this reason, people climbing after you should hopefully know to slide their draw between the carabiner and the wall when clipping.

In a recent development, on coastal routes, solid gate carabiners will eventually corrode shut, requiring a saw to remove. On the coast, only leave wiregates unless the wall is frequently trafficked. Speaking of difficult to remove, quick links should not be left on lead bolts. They require someone else to stop their climbing to use two hands to clean up after you. They are not cheaper than carabiners, unless you use the cheap hardware store ones that rust over and eventually require a saw to remove. If you must leave something, it must be a carabiner. Buy a stick clip and you’ll get an endless supply of free carabiners!

Recent findings suggest that let’s say we’ve decided to leave a draw. Now just stay connected with your trolley and continue lowering to the ground. The system will experience extra friction with the zigzag in the rope, which is nice. If you want to leave just a carabiner, you’ll go in direct to the draw you wish to clean, slack the rope, and clip the carabiner to the bolt above the draw. Then insert the climber’s end of the rope to the carabiner. Take hard, then remove the draw, and lower.

Industry observers note that with both of these methods, you can still retrieve your draw/carabiner. The fastest, and sketchiest way to do so is to solo up to the first bolt (and back down). If it’s easy climbing and you’re comfortable, it does get the job done quickly. Otherwise, removing the draw with a stick clip is much safer, and won’t take too much longer.

Now let’s dig into a couple specialized scenarios.

It has been revealed that technically, the advice that follows on reclaiming the quickdraw from the first bolt safely is part of cleaning a route on the way down. But it involves some niche skills. So, let’s imagine you don’t want to leave a carabiner or draw behind on the first bolt. And you also don’t want to solo up to the first bolt, nor do you have a stick clip. If it’s a big, rounded glue-in, you can do a lower-out off the first bolt. In short, a lower-out is using a length of rope to do a secondary lower that safely equalizes the climber onto the plumb line. The goal here is to cancel out the swing potential, not to lower to the ground, so the belayer should hold tight. Do not lower the climber until the lower-out is complete or you’ll use up more rope on the lower-out than expected.

There are several ways to set up a lower-out. My favorite method? Give myself a huge tail on a figure-8 on a bight when cleaning the anchor. I make that tail double the length of the distance from the bolt to the object I might hit on a swing. When I arrive at that bolt, I go in direct. Then I unclip the trolley and ask my belayer to relocate under the anchor so they don’t swing. Once they’ve taken hard, I pass the extra long tail through the bolt, tension the extra tail, unclip my attachment to the bolt, lower myself out, then pull the rope through the bolt.

According to recent reports, lower-outs can be done with a knot on the end of the lower-out strand or without. Remember, you should always have the knot in the end of the belayer’s strand! Having a knot on the lower-out chord can keep you from lowering off the end and taking a bad swing if the chord comes up short. However, other times, skipping the knot can sometimes be safer (more on that in a minute). This is where stopping and analyzing is important.

Sources indicate that lower-outs can be done with and without a belay device. If it is a pure roof or horizontal traverse, I will use a belay device to lower-out as the forces are significant. This also puts a lot of friction (wear and tear) on the hangers, and should be done sparingly. If the angle is less extreme, I often prefer to lower-out by hand without a belay device. With this method, it is absolutely imperative that the belayer does not lower the climber until the lower-out is complete. Otherwise, the force on your hands will go from very comfortable to dangerous.

But, why on earth would I ever prefer not using a belay device? If your lower-out chord is a tad short, finishing the lower-out by hand is often necessary to maximize your reach before letting go of the chord. The most dangerous option is to use a belay device and no knot; the issue being that it is very difficult to lower without your back facing the wall you’re trying to avoid hitting. Additionally, transitioning from lowering with the device to lowering by hand is risky. The safest thing is to knot the end, lower-out with an assisted braking belay device, hang on the device to clear the knot, then finish lowering by hand. If the pendulum angle is mild enough, I’ll skip those first steps and lower the whole way by hand.

Sources indicate that if you use the lower-out method, make sure you have extra rope, as well as a knot in the belayer’s end of the rope. I’d recommend practicing lower-outs in no-risk scenarios first to understand the forces. You may be surprised how easy and safe it can be to two-hand the rope. After the lower-out, simply pull the rope to retrieve. If the belayer avoids lowering during the lower-out, the rope friction on the bolt is minimal and wear and tear on the bolt is non-existent. Still, it’s better to avoid making a habit out of this.

But what if it’s not a fat rounded glue-in bolt? In that case, I’d highly recommend against a lower-out due to the rubbing of the rope on the sharper hanger. In this case, I would do a rappel-out. You’d rig it the same as a lower-out, but you set up your extra tail as a rappel instead of a lower (find the midpoint of your tail). Similarly, the belayer must avoid the temptation to lower.

According to recent reports, while you are rappelling out, negligible rope pressure exists on the hanger, but you won’t create any tensioned rubbing friction like you would when lowering. When equalized onto the plumb line, you can pull the rope through the bolt hanger just like before. To further lessen any friction of the rope on the hanger while pulling, flick the tail and pull when the rope is lightest. This way, there will be no wear and tear.

Recent findings suggest that let’s say you weren’t planning to do a lower-out or rappel-out. Your belayer can toss you the bottom of the lead line to use just the same. Just make sure that before you untie the stopper knot at the end of the line, that the belayer ties a new stopper knot on their break strand (an overhand on a bight is fine). This requires a bit more rope than the first method, so just be careful.

Sources indicate that but what if we don’t have enough rope for a lower-out and you don’t have the means to retrieve the draw any other way? If the bolt is solid, you can rappel straight through the bolt hanger. Blasphemy! This is clearly a last resort, but if you’re going to do it, you should at least know the best method. Firstly, never lower through a bolt hanger. That creates much more friction on the rope and bolt than a lower-out or pulling the rope after rappelling.

Industry observers note that I personally do not believe pulling the rope after rappelling would cause any wear and tear, especially if it is a fatty rounded glue-in. What about an expansion bolt’s hanger? Recent tests have shown this scenario to hold around 11kN. There is some mild risk to the rope when pulling it due to the sharper edges. Just like the rappel-out, you can flick the end of the rope and pull the rope when it’s lightest. Additionally, having minimal extra rope to pull through the bolt is vital. Rig the rope so its end barely touches the ground.

Lastly, avoid this technique above 15-20 feet off the ground unless it’s an emergency scenario because the rope weight will cause more friction when pulling. And of course, this can all be avoided with a stick clip.

If the bolts are close enough together, it’s often easier to just down-aid the route. The steeper the route, the less I’ll tension the rope. In a full roof with close enough bolts, I won’t tension the rope at all. There’s no need for bulky aiders though. I like to keep a 120cm sling coiled up on a lightweight carabiner permanently on my harness, using draws as a PAS.

Industry observers note that if the route involves a full roof, it’s usually best to just down-lead/back-aid the route. This is the standard method with the massive roof cracks in Canyonlands. If you can bump cams then there’s no need to tension the rope.

Sources indicate that however, this article is about sport climbing. What do you do in a pure roof with spaced out bolts? After running into this scenario many times, I find it easier to do a mix of toprope to clean and jugging the rope. I leave my Grigri on the rope, while the belayer belays with their Grigri, sometimes taking in slack, and sometimes acting as a meat anchor. A Black Diamond grappling hook on the bolt hanger allows me to easily unhook the bolt and take the swing.

Speaking of getting creative, let’s wrap up with what will likely be one of the more controversial takes in this article. I’ve often found the fastest, safest (if you pay attention), and easiest (overall for the team) method is for the climber and belayer to both clean simultaneously. I can’t outright recommend it, unless you have a great attention to detail and years of experience with all of the previous techniques, as well as a variety of other techniques. But I’m including it for those climbing veterans who want to help their partners clean faster and easier.

I generally jump to this method if cleaning the lower part of the route on the way down would be a nuisance or dangerous, but cleaning the top on lower is no-problem. First, I tie off the brake strand on my Grigri. Then, in order to lower the climber, I will climb up the route. I go up, they go down. In doing so, they cancel out much of my weight. If the climbing is hard, I’ll just jug up to the first bolt, clip in, and lower them to their next bolt. We both clean our respective bolts at our leisure. The only communication needed is for the climber to call the standard, “lower” and “hold.”.

The climber should stop cleaning one bolt before (above) entering any dangerous swing potential. Once they’ve hit that point, they just hang in space as the belayer continues to ascend with a mix of free, aid, and ascending as they clean. Of course, the belayer should tie backup knots when appropriate.

According to recent reports, once the belayer reaches that final draw left on the wall, they should double check that they are in fact above the danger swing potential and take the swing. If the belayer is still in the dangerous swing potential zone, they can use their brake strand to perform a lower-out. Then the belayer can lower themselves, and then the climber, to the ground. This method is fast and very efficient. It’s also nice for the tired climber who doesn’t want to clean the whole route. Just go about it very carefully and thoughtfully.

It has been revealed that see? Cleaning steep routes doesn’t have to be a huge nuisance. If these techniques are all too much, just remember your safety comes first. Play it safe and leave a carabiner or a draw anytime. Yes, it’s not ideal, but carabiners are much cheaper than broken legs.

Sources indicate that some people book a luxury hotel for the weekend. Others would rather throw a tent in the car and figure out where they’re sleeping later. If you have one of the latter on your holiday shopping list, we’ve got you covered. Below are the best camping gifts that will make their time outside a bit more comfortable—even if they swear they don’t care about that. From the practical gear they’ll use on every trip to the fun extras that let them have their creature comforts, these presents will have them plotting their getaway ASAP.

In a recent development, A good pair of hiking socks is always appreciated, but these come with a little extra feel-good factor. Made with 70 percent organic cotton and a cushioned footbed, Conscious Step socks are comfortable enough for long days on the trail (or lazy ones around camp). Even better, purchases support the National Parks Conservation Association, which works to protect America’s public lands.

It has been revealed that this interactive water bottle doubles as an excuse to strategy their next big camping trip. It comes with 63 illustrated, water-resistant stickers representing every national park in the U.S., so they can track where they’ve visited as they go. Since it’s a Nalgene, it’s also durable and featherlight, perfect for hanging from backpacks and gear bags.

This is the ideal gift for the person who considers coffee a nonnegotiable, regardless of how far they’ve wandered from civilization. This compact brewer is roughly the size of a thermos and makes hot coffee and cold brew concentrate in minutes. Simply add finely ground coffee and hot or cold water, let it brew, then use the hand press to dispense a concentrated shot into the included carafe. With no plugs and no charging required, they can throw it in their bag and go.

Camp chairs are great, but they’re not always the easiest things to lug around. This compact stool weighs just 1.2 pounds, folds down to 7.5 inches, and has a swiveling seat that lets you turn without having to pick up and reposition the whole thing. It supports up to 260 pounds, too, which is impressive for its size.

In a recent development, this is a particularly useful piece of gear for any camper who wants to cut down on what they’re carrying. Hydrapak’s collapsible flask has a built-in filter that removes common waterborne bacteria and parasites, allowing hikers to refill from water sources along the trail. It weighs just 4.1 ounces and packs completely flat when empty. It’s a great option for biking, hiking, paddling, and even traveling through sketchy airport bathrooms.

It has been revealed that A headlamp is one of those camping essentials you don’t fully appreciate until you’re stumbling around camp in the dark. The Storm delivers up to 550 lumens with adjustable brightness, three different colored modes (red, blue, and green) to preserve night vision, and a waterproof-rated IPX7 construction that can handle rain and snow. It also has a lock mode to prevent it from accidentally turning on in your pack and draining the batteries before you even reach camp.

If you want your family and friends to experience comfort in camp, look no further than this hammock. The kit has everything someone needs to set up between two trees, including polyester straps and iron carabiners. The Portable Hammock has a weight capacity of 551 pounds and it exhibits both the toughness and user-friendliness that Jeep is known for: It’s made from durable nylon and conveniently packs away into a built-in pouch that doubles as a pocket when the hammock is set up.

Recent findings suggest that there are hundreds of camp slippers on the market, but few are as truly warm or versatile as Glerups. Made from 100 percent natural wool, they’re naturally temperature-regulating and odor-resistant, so feet stay comfortable without getting swampy. The slip-on design makes them easy to kick off tent-side, while the rubber sole handles dirt, mud, and slippery moss with ease.

In a recent development, finicky sleepers will love this sleeping bag. The Kelty Eclipse skips the traditional zipper in favor of a clever wraparound design that campers spread out when they’re hot or cocoon themself when they’re cold. What it lacks in zippers it makes up for in thoughtful details, including a self-sealing foot vent, oversized hood to keep pillows in place, and internal pockets. It’s also rated to 15 degrees Fahrenheit, so it’s built for more than just balmy summer nights.

A good outdoor blanket earns its keep in just about every situation, and Yeti’s Lowlands is designed to handle more than one night under the stars. Its waterproof, puncture-resistant bottom keeps damp ground from seeping through, while the cushioned top provides a comfortable place to sit, stretch out, or let the dog settle in. Roll it up for transport, then bring it out for everything from picnics to beach days to tailgates.

Industry observers note that if their cooking kit is just a recycled takeout container and one random spork, please get them this Gerber set. The 16-piece set includes a saute pan, stock pot, hot pad, and tableware for four people, giving them everything they need to make and serve a proper meal without cobbling together a kitchen from mismatched gear. When they’re finished, everything nests together for easy packing until the next time they need it.

These are the pants they’ll put on once at camp and have absolutely no interest in taking off, especially in colder temps. The Fernos pair a cozy insulated interior with a water-resistant exterior, making them ideal for chilly mornings, lounging around the campsite, or layering over a base layer when snow starts to fall. In other words, they’re very durable sweatpants.

Industry observers note that this is about as close as campers can get to bringing their mattress into the woods. The 3.9-inch memory foam pad is thick, supportive, and genuinely comfortable—more proper bed than half-deflated sleeping pad situation. It’s not designed for backpacking (don’t try to carry this on a thru-hike), but it’s portable enough to toss in the car for weekend camping trips. It rolls up tightly for storage and transport and self-inflates when unrolled, making set-up a breeze.

One of the best things about Luno’s car camping mattresses is that they’re not reserved for people with tricked-out 4x4s. The Air Pro is designed to fit a wide range of vehicles, with custom-fit options for dozens of makes and models. This particular kit includes a luxe inflatable mattress, air pump, fitted sheet, pillow, and window screen set that turns their backseat into a dreamy place to sleep. Simply put in their car’s year, make, and model and choose their window size for the gift of spontaneous overnights and long road trips.

This is for the camp chef who thinks camping dinner should involve way more than hot dogs and s’mores. The Gozney Tread is a portable pizza oven that heats up to 950°F and cooks a delicious pie in about a minute. Its compact design makes it shockingly easy to transport and it runs on propane, so they won’t need to fuss with building a fire. Sure, it’s a bit of a splurge for the campsite, but the lucky recipient will have no trouble convincing their camping buddies it’s worth the extra trunk space.

Recent findings suggest that all campers know that a tent you can properly stand up in is the gift that keeps on giving. The Aurora Highrise has near-vertical walls and a roomy interior that comfortably accommodates up to six people, making it a good pick for families or groups who don’t love sleeping elbow-to-elbow. Large windows and doors let in plenty of light and airflow, while Nightlight Pockets let headlamps and flashlights cast an ambient glow. There’s also a generous vestibule for stashing muddy boots, camping chairs, and anything else that needs protection overnight.

#114304. On Climbing Mount Robson’s Emperor Face Alone

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (858 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Climbing ↗ Open Full Page

On Climbing Mount Robson’s Emperor Face Alone

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (858 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Climbing

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that high on the Emperor Ridge of Mount Robson, enjoying lunch in the sun.
  • In a recent development, there is a cinema up north.
  • In September of 2026 I soloed Infinite Patience on the Emperor Face of Mount Robson.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that high on the Emperor Ridge of Mount Robson, enjoying lunch in the sun. (Photo: Anton Korsun).

In a recent development, there is a cinema up north. Beyond the rising northern star, beyond the Icefields Parkway, and far beyond the chaos and clamor of the Banff Mountain Film Festival—it is built in the image of a gothic cathedral and shrouded in storm. This cinema operates year round. It has no dress code, schedule, or rules on serving alcohol to minors. Inside, every visitor watches their own film: Some see triumph and elation. Others see despair, retreat, or a kaleidoscope of rock and ice before the front doors shut forever and the silver screen goes deathly black. Yet others simply stand alone in its great white hall, listening to the sound of silence and watching mountain ranges stretch to the horizon like limbs of a great white spider.

This is a film review of sorts. In September of 2026 I soloed Infinite Patience on the Emperor Face of Mount Robson. I’ve been asked to write about it. I’ve been asked why I haven’t posted anything on social media or pontificated my radness to the press. Frankly, it’s because I am a rather poor film critic.

There is no doubt in my mind that alpine climbing is more art than sport.

If I were to ask you—how did Usain Bolt run 100 meters in 9.58 seconds?

“Well, he moved his legs quite fast,” you might say.

But can you tell me how Voytek Kurtyka and Robert Schauer suffered up the Shining Wall of Gasherbrum IV (7,925m) in a 10-day sleep-and-food-deprived push? Or how Steve House and Marko Prezelj clawed their way to the summit of the North Twin with one missing boot and two coreshot ropes? Because I can’t.

It has been revealed that I sit in awe of the performers on stage as they pull another rabbit from their hats or escape the icy chains of some far-flung north face yet again. The beauty of alpinism is similar to the beauty of theater, dance, and stage magic—an illusion of wizardry brought about by true mastery of the performers.

However, while similar, alpinism and theater are not the same. Climbing has no audience and no stage. Climbing media has both. In recent times it has become too easy to convince ourselves that perception equals participation—that by clicking that “follow” button or watching that film we can stand in the shoes of the artist. But we can’t. Because to believe otherwise would be to mistake climbing as performing art for climbing as performance art. The former is the way the ascent is portrayed in words, photographs, or film. The latter—what was seen, felt, thought and feared in the moment—is privy only to the performers themselves.

It has been revealed that I often find myself wondering about how the way an ascent is communicated influences the audience’s perception of what actually happened. This can range from flying in a substantial-budget film crew, to more subtle cues, like how a photo was cropped for Instagram, or whether one was shared at all. These words themselves are guilty, although I try to segregate my act of climbing from my act of writing about it.

Sources indicate that my reluctance to share much about the climb stems from a fear that this blade is sharp on both sides—that the audience’s media-driven perception can in turn influence the climber’s own perception of the experience. Much like how the behaviour of quantum particles changes when they’re observed, climbers too, change our behaviour. Our egos feed off validation. Our eye becomes drawn to the viewfinder or to the stopwatch. We feel the presence of the audience cut through the ridgetop wind. We hear their applause over the crash of séracs in the distance.

I watched The Alpinist on the big screen when it was first released. While I never met Marc-André Leclerc, it left me feeling that much more went unsaid—that the real movie of his life was seen through his eyes only. A movie no one can rewind.

Sources indicate that but anything is possible in cinema. In his account of Infinite Patience, Marc-André describes being unable to take a photo of a beautiful sunrise because his camera batteries had failed—“the shadow of Mt. Robson extending forever into the horizon against a red sky.”.

From my sleeping perch high on the Emperor Ridge, I awoke to the same scene. Waves of red and gold crashed against the east face of Whitehorn Mountain while Robson’s summit pyramid shadowed the valley thousands of feet below. Was this movie magic or something more? Feeling as if I was suddenly not alone, I pulled out my phone in disbelief and took that photo. We can’t rewind each other’s films, but sometimes life lets us watch them together.

Nonetheless, I’m saddened to be left alone with my experience. My words are a lousy companion and my photographs are only worth a thousand lousy words. All I know is that I watched my film on the summit of Mount Robson. Where are you watching yours?

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1069 w)

Zion Draws The Crowds—These 3 Nearby Parks Are Where to Escape Them

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1069 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Backpacker

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Just beyond Zion lie some truly incredible desert landscapes to wander without the crowds.
  • Entry queues and crowded trails come with the territory at bucket-list national parks like Zion.
  • But I’ll be honest: On my recent trip to Zion, the trails felt more like a conga line than a wilderness escape.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Just beyond Zion lie some truly incredible desert landscapes to wander without the crowds. (Photo: Arrterra via Getty).

Entry queues and crowded trails come with the territory at bucket-list national parks like Zion. With nearly 5 million visitors in 2025, it ranked as the second-most visited national park in the U.S. Once you make it through the entry gate, though, the payoff is real. Visitors walk beneath towering Navajo sandstone cliffs and wade the Virgin River deep into The Narrows. If luck’s on your side, you might even win the permit lottery to hike to Angels Landing.

But I’ll be honest: On my recent trip to Zion, the trails felt more like a conga line than a wilderness escape. I was more paranoid than peaceful, constantly stepping aside and watching my footing as I squeezed past other hikers. The incredible beauty of the park draws equally incredible crowds.

The good news is you don’t have to fight for elbow room to soak in Zion’s beauty. Its neighboring state parks, wildernesses, and national forests get a fraction of the attention, but are just as jaw-dropping. Explore the surrounding Greater Zion region, and you’ll unlock hikes through red rock without the gridlock.

Head beyond Zion for these underrated hiking spots instead.

It has been revealed that distance from Zion: 1 hour (West) Entrance fee: $15 per vehicle Best for: Hikers seeking desert variety without a grueling trek. Petrified dunes, sandstone cliffs, slot canyons, and hikeable lava tubes, all in one park.

Sources indicate that if Snow Canyon State Park were a DJ, it’d spin a killer geological mashup of 180-million-year-old petrified dunes, Jurassic-period sandstone escarpments, and ancient river-carved slot canyons. The drop: cavernous, jet-black lava tubes you can hike into (headlamp recommended). The park packs a huge punch of diverse terrain you rarely see all in one place. It’s especially family-friendly and a good fit for more casual hikers who want photo-worthy views without a grueling trek.

Catch the park’s greatest hits in one go by linking up the Butterfly Trail, Lava Flow Overlook, West Canyon Overlook, and the Petrified Dunes Loop. The roughly 3-mile loop connects the park’s most notable features. Hikers will see ancient lava flows, winding slickrock passages, and sweeping views down into West Canyon. The petrified dunes along the route steal the show. Hikers walk over rolling hills frozen in time while swirling stripes of orange, cream, and crimson dance underfoot.

Looking for more technical hiking? Tackle the trek to Deidre Peak. The 7.4-mile out-and-back climbs nearly 1,500 feet in elevation and requires a Class 3-4 scramble over rugged sandstone outcrops. The trail crosses into the larger Red Cliffs Desert Reserve, a conservation area protected as a sanctuary for the native Mojave desert tortoise.

Distance from Zion: 1 hour (West) Entrance fee: $5 per vehicle Best for: Hikers and BLM land lovers seeking seclusion and solitude.

Beyond Snow Canyon sprawls Red Cliffs National Conservation Area. The nearly 45,000 acres of BLM land sits within the larger Red Cliffs Desert Reserve at the crossroads of the Mojave Desert, Great Basin, and Colorado Plateau. Here you’ll find a mix of plants and wildlife from all three regions. There are two endangered wildflowers that grow only in this corner of Utah: the dwarf bear poppy and Shivwits milkvetch. Both bloom in spring, with peak overlap in late April and early May. Then there’s southern Utah’s classic red sandstone stretching as far as the eye can see.

Popular out-and-back hikes like the 3.5-mile Elephant Arch Trail and 1.6-mile Red Reef Trail show how water and wind erosion turn sandstone landscapes into works of art. Elephant Arch earned its name from a distinct sandstone outcropping that looks uncannily like a trunk, head, and ears. Along the Red Reef Trail, hikers skirt massive, smooth sandstone bowls. These turn into swimming holes during spring rain and monsoon season, which runds July through September.

The 5-mile Black Gulch and Yellow Knolls Loop drops through a boulder-strewn gulch of dark volcanic rock, then rolls over yellow sandstone knolls. Hikers can also link the Red Reef and Prospector Trails to create a 10.5-mile loop requiring some scrambling and route-finding through remote backcountry canyons. On the return leg, wide views open up to the Pine Valley Mountains in the north, often capped with snow in winter and early spring.

Distance from Zion: 1 hour 15 minutes (Northeast) Entrance fee: None Best for: Hikers looking for trail variety that showcases Utah’s finest terrain.

It has been revealed that the state’s largest national forest shows off a completely different side of southern Utah. Dixie National Forest sprawls across nearly 2 million acres, rising from the desert valley around St. George to peaks above 11,000 feet. Sagebrush, pinyon, and juniper give way to aspen groves and conifer forests as you climb. The higher and farther you hike, the more surprises you’ll find: trout-filled mountain lakes, towering hoodoo spires, and the chance to spot Utah prairie dogs in the wild.

Dixie gives hikers a taste of the same pink-and-orange Claron limestone that made Bryce Canyon famous. The difference? Here, thick stands of ponderosa pine grow right up against the hoodoos. Plus, the trails see a fraction of the foot traffic, so you’ll have the views practically to yourself.

If you want more hoodoo action, check out Thunder Mountain Trail. It winds through what feels like a bite-sized Bryce Canyon. The out-and-back trail climbs more than 1,700 feet over 8.6 miles. You’re rewarded with an unforgettable trek through a maze of spires. For an even more awe-inspiring experience, hike early or late in the day, when low sun turns the Claron limestone a vibrant orange.

According to recent reports, looking for a more Zion-esque experience? Ashdown Gorge Trail echoes the Narrows, minus the permits, rental gear, and crowds. It travels 10 miles from the alpine rim of Cedar Breaks to a creek-carved canyon where red rock walls close in overhead. Heads up: There are two popular ways to hike Ashdown Gorge. You can do an out-and-back that starts at the bottom and heads up into the narrows (recommended), or a point-to-point that requires a shuttle.

For a longer, relatively flat dayhike, opt for the 11-mile Navajo Lake Loop. The trail circles its namesake, peeking in and out of dense pine, fir, and aspen forest, with shoreline views that make it easy to forget you’re in a red rock wonderland.

The 10,000-BTU Zempire Stealth Jet Twin isn’t the most powerful camp stove we’ve ever tested, but it is the slimmest two-burner we’ve ever tested, making it a sweet gift for car campers who value trunk space and camp cuisine alike. It has been revealed that when backpackers want to cut down on pack weight, they often opt for titanium cookware and accessories, as the metal offers an unbeatable strength-to-weight ratio. Smaller pieces, like Snow Peak’s iconic sporks, are a backpacker’s dream stocking stuffer, while drinkware and cooksets are destined to become prized possessions.

Snow Peak Titanium Spork - Long.

It has been revealed that there are a million gizmos and gadgets out there for the espresso fanatics, the drip disciples, the press-and-plunge crowd. But what about the nitro lovers? Behold: the Cumulus Coffee Machine. An all-in-one robot for chilled coffee lovers that brings barista-grade bevies into the comfort of your own home, the machine has three settings that allow you to convert Cumulus pods into iced espresso, crisp cold brew, and creamy nitro. The nitro setting is particularly rad, as the Cumulus sources nitrogen from ambient air—no nitrogen cartridges required. And there’s no ice required, either, as the machine self-chills. This is a dream gift for any cold brew connoisseur, but especially those who order nitro on the regular.

Ben Zartman Splices Climbing Slings In His Garage. They’re the Best I’ve Ever Used.

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1117 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Climbing

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that ben Zartman at work splicing slings in his garage.
  • When Ben Zartman learned to climb near Mexico City in the early 1990s, no one he knew could afford climbing gear.
  • “All of us were poor, and all the gear was imported and so expensive,” he claims.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that ben Zartman at work splicing slings in his garage. (Photo: Courtesy Ben Zartman).

When Ben Zartman learned to climb near Mexico City in the early 1990s, no one he knew could afford climbing gear.

“All of us were poor, and all the gear was imported and so expensive,” he claims. “Most of the guys at the crag were sewing their own shoes or making their own cams.” Backpacks, harnesses, quickdraws—if they could sew it themselves, they did. At the time, Zartman was in high school. He didn’t have a job, but he did have a knack for making stuff. It never occurred to him that doing so might be sketchy until he arrived in Yosemite for the first time in 1995 and partners refused to climb on his rack. They were astonished he’d made his own gear. He was astonished that they’d bought theirs.

Recent findings suggest that later that year, when a government shutdown forced Zartman out of Joshua Tree, he hitchhiked to San Diego and bummed a ride to Baja with some sailors. Over the next few years, he split his time between big walls and boats, getting better at both kinds of rigging all the while. Then he got married, had three daughters, and spent five years sailing around the world on a boat he’d built himself. Eventually, he got work in a rigging shop in Rhode Island. He spliced custom slings for workaday sailors, then for open-ocean racing boats.

“At one point, I was sitting in the shop, splicing these high-end Dyneema loops, and I thought, man, if I had these in Yosemite, I would have been the coolest kid at the lodge cafeteria,” he states. And he likely would have: the spliced, covered loops used in sailing are seamless: no bar tacks or stitching. Instead, one end of the loop is woven into the other like a snake eating its tail. When you pull, the ends suction against each other (Zartman compares it to a finger-trap toy), making the loop stronger under load than bartacked Dyneema.

“The idea fomented for a while in my mind, and in 2021 I started reaching out to every climbing gear manufacturer I could think of,” Zartman says. Letters and samples went out to Black Diamond, Metolius, Sterling, and others, asking them if they’d be interested in partnering on a product. Hardly anyone responded.

Sources indicate that so Zartman did what he’d always done: he took the DIY approach. In 2023, he released his company, Zartman Rigging. He joined the UIAA, mailed in slings for lab testing, and registered for UIAA labels. Once his gear was certified, the renowned gear shop IME, in North Conway, New Hampshire, started selling it. Rock and Snow in New Paltz, New York, and IME in Salt Lake City, Utah, were next. As his following grew, so did his offerings: a featherlight personal anchor system, seamless rappel back-ups, a rope-carabiner alternative called the Dreamlink, and a tiny rappel plate designed for 6-mm cord. The ideas come from Zartman’s experience climbing Yosemite walls; the materials come from his time on boats.

In a recent development, “The research and development budget in the [sailboat] racing scene is so big,” he says. “It’s a great place to take technology from. I’m at that edge—I make ropes for the fanciest racing boats in the world, so I’m able to bring that into the climbing world pretty quickly.”.

According to recent reports, the results are wild. The Dreamlink has a breaking strength of 43 kN (or, rather, he tested it up to 42 kN in a UIAA lab, and that’s when it broke their machine). The seamless runners are tagged 24 kN but break at 27kN. A fancy UV coating makes them essentially sun-proof. They don’t expire like other soft goods; you only have to retire them if the core becomes exposed. I have a double-length seamless runner that I use for building anchors and extending rappels. No bartack means easy setup, it racks well, and it’s pretty light. (Most traditionally manufactured Dyneema slings are tagged at 22kN. Mammut’s 120-centimeter Contact Sling weighs 28 grams, while Zartman’s version is 32 grams, the same as Black Diamond’s Infinity Cord.).

Industry observers note that zartman has a strong social media fan club, but he has plenty of critics too. Mountain Project commenters, he mentioned, can be particularly vicious. Many scoff at the idea of a soft shackle or a seamless runner as gimmicky or unsafe. He’s not too bothered.

It has been revealed that “Ray Jardine got scolded by all the Valley locals when he showed up with Friends,” he notes, citing the first-ever cams. When other companies started making camming devices in the ‘80s, Jardine’s critics were forced to bite their tongues. Zartman is seeing a similar arc with his own gear. Several other climbing brands have started marketing soft shackles similar to Zartman’s Dreamlink. And in 2025, Black Diamond released its Infinity Cord, a Dyneema sling that uses the same bartack-free construction as Zartman’s and the same covered-loop splicing technique that sailors have used for decades. Black Diamond called it a “breakthrough in the evolution of cordelette engineering.”.

Recent findings suggest that zartman says he’s unaffected by the newly introduced competition. “If there are people copying the concept, that’s good because that means the concept is good,” he says. In the meantime, he’s keeping his head down, focused on fulfilling orders and prototyping his next batch of inventions.

Recent findings suggest that zartman Rigging is gaining recognition, albeit slowly. Zartman does no paid advertising; about 80 percent of his business comes from Instagram. His top-shelf pricing likely tempers growth as well. For context, a 120-centimeter Zartman Rigging sling is $63, versus $40 for Black Diamond’s Infinity Cord or $14 for a basic Dyneema Trango runner of the same length.

It has been revealed that “Because I make everything out of the nicest materials and by hand, it’s the most expensive gear on the market. It’s a luxury brand,” he says. “Which is ironic given that I started in Mexico with my own homemade climbing shoes.”.

Still, he produces enough to keep busy. Recently, he was able to hire one of his daughters part-time to help him splice, tag, and quality-test each product. He’s now a member of the UIAA safety commission, helping the organization design newly introduced testing protocols around skinny ropes and other novel forms of cord. He’s shipping to Alaska and Hawaii. People have started recognizing him in gear shops and at crags. Things are taking off—despite what Mountain Projectors may say.

“To a lot of people’s surprise,” he laughs, “I’ve sold a lot of gear.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Photo: Joern Siegroth / Getty Images).

As firefighters continue to battle a nearby blaze, Shenandoah National Park is implementing rigid fire restrictions due to exceptionally dry conditions and heightened wildfire risks going into Thanksgiving week.

In a Facebook post park officials explained: “These restrictions protect public safety given the elevated risk of wildland fires throughout the park. Shenandoah National Park, Skyline Drive and other facilities and services remain open as scheduled.”.

According to recent reports, under these new restrictions, visitors to the area will have to rethink their cooking plans since they are temporarily unable to build, attend, or maintain open fires anywhere within the park’s boundaries, including in established pits, grates, and in grills. These regulations also apply to picnic areas, shelters, and huts in the park.

These rules also impact backpackers who rely on portable stoves while recreating in the area. Liquid and wood-fuel camp stoves cannot be used within the park until further notice. At the moment, campers can still use canister stoves like Jet Boils and MSR Pocket Rockets.

Recent findings suggest that this announcement came just one day after the White Oak Flat Fire erupted on U.S. Forest Service land about 50 miles southwest of Shenandoah National Park. Since Friday, the fire has grown to 1,800 acres, with 49% containment. So far, 131 wildland personnel have responded to the fire including handcrews, wildland engines, bulldozers and two helicopters. Wildland firefighters are using active suppression strategies to contain the fire. No evacuations have been reported, and a cause for the fire has yet to be released.

The NPS identifies two primary wildfire seasons in Shenandoah that run from February to May and October through December. Wildfires are relatively common in Virginia during the month of November although the frequency and impacted acreage vary by season and seasonal driving factors like low humidity and breezy weather.

Shenandoah park officials expect these restrictions to remain in place until the region receives enough precipitation to reduce fire risks.

Frankfurt, Germany (Photo: Lufthansa).

Nearly everybody visits Europe in summer. That’s no exaggeration: Half of all international inbound arrivals to the continent happen between June and September, with hotels, trails, attractions, and city streets swelling with nearly three times the people you’d encounter in January.

It has been revealed that that’s good news for winter fans. Seasonal highlights like festivals and craft markets and storybook scenery give winter travelers a whole different world to discover. Thanks to Lufthansa’s daily flights to its German city hubs from 18 U.S. cities coast to coast, enjoying the holiday traditions and empty museums requires very little effort. Just say yes.

Here’s how to get started on planning your winter getaway.

According to recent reports, frankfurt’s winter markets are best enjoyed on foot, as you’ll wind through more than 230 stalls. Fuel up for the walk with a Bethmännchen, the city’s traditional marzipan pastry, and warm up with a mug of hot apple wine before tracing your way along the Main River. Explore the famous Palmengarten glasshouses for a botanical escape to tropical, desert, and alpine environments, all within the urban core. Beyond the city, enjoy winter silence and peace on hundreds of marked winter trails crisscrossing the snow-dusted Taunus woods.

Industry observers note that see why this iconic city deserves its reputation as the international capital for modern culture. Stroll from the treed paths of the Tiergarten to Berlin’s many bridges (more than Venice). Sculptors and architects have turned all of Berlin into an open-air museum, but when the weather turns, you can duck into the galleries peppering the Auguststraße and Potsdamer Straße. Stay fueled at neighborhood cafés inspired by international cuisines, and join the late-night reveling at concerts and dance clubs. (New Year’s Eve is a can’t-miss holiday.).

Sources indicate that elsewhere in Europe, there’s more to love about winter. In Italy, explore the eye-popping Dolomites, or visit Renaissance landmarks in Florence without the crowds. If you time it right, experience Venice’s Carnevale in late January and early February. In France, the Champs-Élysées Christmas market ends its decade-long absence this season, bringing 200 chalets to the famous Paris avenue. Prefer a warmer winter break? Head to Greece, where you can have Athens—and its ancient historic sites—practically to yourself. That’s easy to say yes to.

Whether you want to explore holiday magic in Germany, visit landmarks in Italy, or enjoy a warmer winter in Greece, Lufthansa gets you there.

Sources indicate that the Lufthansa Group is a global aviation group with over 100,000 employees from 164 nations. In 2025, it carried more than 135 million passengers and generated €39.6 billion in revenue. Its largest segment, Passenger Airlines, includes the core airline Lufthansa and other leading European carriers, complemented by Logistics, MRO, IT, and Lufthansa Aviation Training.

I wish this shoe came in a slightly wider last.

Industry News: Hike to Over 100 Arches, Hidden Waterfalls, and Towering Cliffs in Kentucky’s Largest Canyon

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (839 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Backpacker

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The trail to Natural Bridge will work up a sweat, but the effort is rewarded.
  • According to recent reports, while thoroughbred horse racing and barrel-aged bourbon have made Kentucky famous, the state is also home to biodiverse forests and geologically rich mountains.
  • This ancient canyon spans tens of thousands of acres in eastern/central Kentucky.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The trail to Natural Bridge will work up a sweat, but the effort is rewarded. (Photo: Michelle Polizzi).

According to recent reports, while thoroughbred horse racing and barrel-aged bourbon have made Kentucky famous, the state is also home to biodiverse forests and geologically rich mountains. Western Appalachia is a hiker’s paradise, with hundreds of miles of trails, accessing some of the Bluegrass State’s most striking landscapes—and the Red River Gorge is one of its crown jewels.

This ancient canyon spans tens of thousands of acres in eastern/central Kentucky. The powerful Red River carved the Gorge millions of years ago, creating an outdoor playground of cliffs, creeks, waterfalls, and sculpted rock. It has more than 60 official hiking trails and more sandstone arches than anywhere else in the eastern U.S.

Here’s what to see, where to hike, and how to play if you’ve just got one weekend in Kentucky’s Red River Gorge.

Industry observers note that every first-time visitor to the Red River Gorge must visit Gray’s Arch—no exceptions. This massive natural sandstone structure will give you a crash course in the area’s unique topography, including a diverse hardwood forest, massive rock outcroppings, and steep staircases built directly into the hillsides.

Sources indicate that while most visitors stick to the 2.5-mile out-and-back trail to Gray’s Arch before turning around, it’s worth extending your hike to 5.8 miles on the Gray’s Arch Long Loop Trail. This route takes you past the crowds that gather beneath Gray’s Arch. It winds deeper into the canyon, through the cool, damp forest, over creeks, and beneath looming rock overhangs that still hold Indigenous petroglyphs.

Whittleton Campground has a free day-use lot with a trailhead accessing multiple hikes. Two trails lead to the Whittleton Arch, and another goes to Hensen’s Arch. Try the standard USFS Whittleton Trail, a 2-mile loop that starts and ends at the campground. Or take the longer Whittleton Branch Trail #216. This 4.8-mile out-and-back accesses the arch and follows a creek for most of its length.

From the campground, you can also hike the Hensen’s Arch Trail. In less than a mile, you’ll reach a second sandstone arch and a deep sinkhole where you can descend into the Earth via a set of metal stairs.

It has been revealed that if you’re still feeling adventurous after you hike, head to SUP Kentucky for a Crystal Kayak and SUP Glow Tour, where you’ll paddle underground into a submerged former limestone mine. Thanks to limestone’s natural filtration properties, the water is astoundingly clear. Watch schools of rainbow trout swim beneath your LED-illuminated translucent kayaks, as colors refract upon the ceiling.

In a recent development, the highlight of Kentucky’s Natural Bridge State Resort Park is the massive natural bridge (for which it’s named). This impressive geologic feature stands 65 feet high and 78 feet in length.

In a recent development, there are several ways to access the arch. Hikers can take the 5.5-mile Natural Bridge and Battleship Rock Trail, which winds past five different trail shelters. Hikers walk beneath some of the country’s tallest tulip poplar trees—some standing more than 150 feet. Natural Bridge is the trail’s climax. You can view the rock formation from numerous vantage points, and even walk across the arch to the lookout point.

It has been revealed that for a longer, more challenging approach, try the 7.5-mile Sand Gap Trail. It can be done as an out-and-back, or connected with Natural Bridge Trail to make a loop.

Sources indicate that for more ridge, arch, and canyon trails, head 30 minutes north of the Natural Bridge State Resort Park to the Auxier Ridge Trailhead. From this hub, hikers can access the 6.0-mile Double Arch Loop, which follows Auxier Ridge and passes Courthouse Rock, Haystack Rock, Double Arch, and Arch of Triumph.

The Star Gap and Skyview Arch Trail also starts at the Auxier Ridge trailhead. This roughly 6-mile out-and-back hike is narrow and woodsy. It includes some overgrown sections and short scrambles with about 1,300 feet of elevation gain. But the effort is rewarded with access to Skyview Arch at the end.

Dispersed camping is allowed around Auxier Ridge. Or check out the Sandstone Drifter, a reservable cliffside treehouse accessed by a suspension bridge. But be warned: climbing its 177-stair floating staircase is a short, steep hike in itself.

It has been revealed that when rock-climbing traffic slows in winter and early spring, the Muir Valley Nature Preserve is a perfect place to see waterfalls at their full splendor. That’s when precipitation is highest, meaning larger, fuller falls and a chance to see giant icicles and frozen cascades of water. A $15 parking fee is required, and visitors must sign a waiver before entering.

Connect Horseshoe Falls, Joe Ponder Falls, Stadium Wall, and Nellie’s Falls to create a moderate, 4.4-mile hiking loop that spans three waterfalls and winds beneath sandstone overhangs. To extend the hike, add Liz’s Arch and Washboard Wall Trail for an additional 1.5 miles, exposing hikers to more arches, cliffs, and several rock-climbing areas.

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (483 w)

Tech Report: Gary Colliver Was a “Major-Hearted” Climber Who Devoted Decades to Yosemite

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gary Colliver on 'Lucky Streaks' (5.10+), a six-pitch trad climb on Fairview Dome in Yosemite, in 1980.
  • Industry observers note that gary Colliver passed away on August 30, 2026, in Denver, Colorado.
  • Throughout his life, Yosemite’s beauty was a current which drew him back, time and time again.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gary Colliver on 'Lucky Streaks' (5.10+), a six-pitch trad climb on Fairview Dome in Yosemite, in 1980. (Photo: Courtesy of Dave Sessions).

Industry observers note that gary Colliver passed away on August 30, 2026, in Denver, Colorado. He was 83. A longtime Yosemite Valley resident, he spent decades caring for the park as a ranger, medic, rescuer, and advocate.

Throughout his life, Yosemite’s beauty was a current which drew him back, time and time again. Colliver discovered climbing in college and soon moved to Camp 4. He met his future wife, Reva, in Tuolumne Meadows, married her in the Yosemite Valley Chapel in 1965, and built a decades-long career serving the park and its visitors.

In the early days of climbing in the Valley, Colliver was a quiet giant. With Richard McCracken and John Evans, he made the fourth ascent of the Nose (5.9 C2; 3,000ft) on El Capitan. He later returned to the route for the film El Capitan (1978), and in 1969, he climbed the Salathé Wall (5.9 C2; 3,500ft) with Chris Jones.

Later, his ambitions also took him beyond Yosemite. In 1964, he and Glen Denny made the first ascent of Jirishanca Norte (19,735ft) in Peru. In 1970, he joined Jones, Bob Cuthbert, and Gray Thompson for the first complete ascent of Mount Adamant’s north ridge in British Columbia. The following year, he participated in the International Himalayan Expedition to Mount Everest, where his team attempted a new route on Everest’s Southwest Face.

To Dave Sessions, Colliver’s second cousin, those accomplishments belonged to an exceptionally modest man. “He was one of the most modest people I ever met in my life. Incredibly soft-spoken,” Sessions said. “Never, never sought out attention or, you know, just very kind-hearted and modest and soft-spoken.”.

Colliver’s work in Yosemite included serving as a wilderness and climbing ranger, park medic, and volunteer firefighter. In 1983, he and two fellow rangers received a Department of the Interior Valor Award for rescuing a visitor from swift water.

His National Park Service colleague Mark Finscher worked alongside him on an early effort to develop a climbing management strategy for the Valley, bringing together interest groups with opposing views on access, bolting, and responsible climbing.

In a recent development, “There were some strong personalities in that group, and Gary did a good job of dealing with that,” Finscher said. Although that initial initiative was never formally signed, Colliver continued working in park planning and compliance. Finscher remembered him as an ally in upholding wilderness protections. “He never took the easy way,” he said.

Recent findings suggest that as a teenager, Sessions had asked Colliver whether he had been scared climbing El Capitan. He answered simply, “No, it was just so beautiful.” But for Colliver, the joy of being in Yosemite extended beyond any particular big wall. “If he was in Yosemite, he was happy,” Sessions said.

12 Gifts That Backpacker’s Editors Actually Want for the Holidays

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1232 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Backpacker

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission.
  • (Photo: Abstract Aerial Art / DigitalVision via Getty).
  • We love outdoor gear, but it’s hard to think of something we need less: Year-round, Backpacker‘s editors test tents, footwear, kitchen gear, and the rest of the latest and greatest hiking equipment to hit the market, and our closets are full to bursting.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy.

(Photo: Abstract Aerial Art / DigitalVision via Getty).

Fractel T-SIERPINKSKI Trucker Hat.

Gossamer Gear Thinlight Foam Rolled Pad.

Harvest Right Countertop 360 Freeze Dryer.

We love outdoor gear, but it’s hard to think of something we need less: Year-round, Backpacker‘s editors test tents, footwear, kitchen gear, and the rest of the latest and greatest hiking equipment to hit the market, and our closets are full to bursting. Still, every once in a while, something comes around that impresses us so much, we’re still thinking about it long after it’s been replaced or passed on to another tester.

We asked our editors to share the gear that’s at the top of their wishlist right now. Some of these wants are modest—a gourmet backpacking meal, a closed-cell foam pad, a trucker hat. Others, like an American-made packraft or a home freeze-dryer, are not. All of it is exceptional. Whether you’re shopping for a hiker who seems like they have everything or adding to your own wish list, this gear is far from ordinary.

Industry observers note that on Backpacker’s recent Editors’ Choice trip along Wisconsin’s Ice Age Trail, we used 10-liter Ursack bear bags to keep our smellables safe, and I fell in love with them. They’re lightweight at just 7.6 ounces, made with bullet-proof Spectra Fabric, and compress as you eat your way through their contents. I wouldn’t throw out my trusty hard canister if I got an Ursack for the holidays, but I’d sure use it a lot. —Will Brendza, Associate Editor.

There are so many flashlights out there, and they range in quality from amazing to shoddy, that I have shied away from actually shopping for one for years. But the LD31 RENEGADE flashlight from Fenix jumped out at me recently. Not only does this puppy pack 3200 lumens in a perfectly sized 5-inch package, but its rechargeable battery also doubles as an emergency external charger and can easily attach to a backpack strap, pocket, or bill of a cap thanks to a two-way clip. On top of all of that, this thing is completely dustproof and waterproof up to 2 meters. —WB.

Sources indicate that I tend to be pretty picky when it comes to outdoor and hiking hats. A lot of them look dorky, use cheap materials, or aren’t comfortable when you wear them. That’s why I was so stoked to find Fractel—a running hat tech giant from Australia that blows most American outdoor hats away. The T-SIERPINKSKI Trucker Hats are stylish, lightweight, breathe well, and come in some wild colorways.—WB.

Leave it to Hyperlite to launch a product I didn’t know I needed, can’t really afford, and desperately want right before the holidays. The brand, known for its ultralight packs and shelters, relaunched its apparel line in 2026, and in November dropped an anorak made with waterproof 3-layer Dyneema. It weighs just 7.5 ounces. Do I need a new anorak? Absolutely not. Would I love to keep this sweet little number in my backpacking kit? You bet. —WB.

It has been revealed that I’m not usually the kind of hiker who’s willing to give up a hip belt on my pack, but the Volpi FastPack 30 was so much fun to use, it made me want to bring less stuff just so I could justify using it. The vest-style carry on this frameless model was comfortable, and stretch storage pockets on the straps and at the bottom (for a rain shell), plus a strap on top for carrying my sleeping pad, made organization simple. —Adam Roy, Editor-in-Chief.

If I have a superpower, it’s being able to sleep anywhere, under any circumstances. Why not take advantage of that? I wouldn’t call Gossamer Gear’s Thinlight pads comfortable—at an eighth of an inch thick, they barely qualify as pads at all—but at just 2.7 ounces, they put even most cut-down closed-cell foam pads to shame when it comes to weight. —AR.

There’s a lot to like about the Soto Windmaster, which our testers picked out as the best backpacking stove of 2026. At just 3.1 ounces, it’s featherweight, and it performs consistently in the worst conditions, putting out a reliable flame without chewing through its gas supply even when it gets breezy. Thanks to its regulated design, it’s a solid pick for winter camping, too—a situation where some of my lightweight canister stoves have struggled. —AR.

Industry observers note that I’ve used a wide variety of inflatable craft during my time at Backpacker, from paddleboards to canoes. But few have impressed me as much as Alpacka’s Chinook, which tracked steadily and sliced through the water on an early-summer trip through Ruby Horsethief Canyon on the Colorado River. With its prominent bow and stern and removable skeg, the Chinook has some kayak DNA in its design, and paddles more like one than some of the squirrelly packrafts I’ve used. At 9.1 pounds, it’s light enough to haul, and in-tube storage and a clip-in point for a deck bag give it enough capacity for deep backcountry expeditions. —AR.

After more than a decade of use, my trusty lightweight tent from Brooks Range Mountaineering (RIP) is about to give up the ghost. (The company closed in 2018, if that tells you anything about how long I’ve been using it.) In my search for a replacement, I got to test out an X-Dome this fall, and I now see what all the fuss is about. This tent has a cult following for a reason: It’s featherweight at 44 ounces but doesn’t skimp on livability; the tall ceiling feels like a luxury for sitting up and changing inside. A simple pitch and details like the large doorways and generous internal pockets put this at the top of my list. —Zoe Gates, Senior Editor.

Food is my love language and there’s nothing better than a consumable gift. I evangelize Stowaway Gourmet freeze dried meals to my backpacking friends any chance I get, because they are just so darn tasty. Perfect for a stocking stuffer, or spring for a 72-meal variety pack to feed your favorite hiker for a year. My faves: Drunken Noodles, Kimchi Jigae, Wild Boar Bacon Stew, and Cereal Killer. —ZG.

The time has come: After years on the trail, I am finally over inflating my sleeping pad manually. Over the years, I’ve tried all the methods, from lung power to foot pumps to inflation sacks. I’m ready to take one dreaded camp chore off my plate. A pad inflator is the height of luxury, and I can’t wait to indulge. —ZG.

If someone really wants to spoil me this year, they’ll invest in a hobby I’ve always wanted to try: freeze drying my own backpacking meals. A dehydrator is an affordable gateway to the world of homemade trail meals, but freeze dryers (larger, more expensive) open up a whole new world of food preservation. Freeze dried meals last longer than dehydrated ones, and maintain better texture and nutritional value—not to mention the wider range of ingredients that hold up to freeze drying. Armed with this appliance, I can spend my whole winter prepping meals for summer backpacking trips—and create some stocking stuffers of my own for the next holiday season. —ZG.
