#114289. How I Sent ‘The Prophet’ and ‘Free Rider’ on El Cap in 18.5 Hours

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2343 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Climbing ↗ Open Full Page

How I Sent ‘The Prophet’ and ‘Free Rider’ on El Cap in 18.5 Hours

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2343 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Climbing

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that left to right: Alex Honnold, Connor Herson, and Tommy Caldwell take a celebratory selfie at the top of 'The Prophet' on El Cap.
  • It has been revealed that my alarm goes off, but I’m already wide awake; I never sleep well before an early start.
  • According to recent reports, established by Leo Houlding and Jason Pickles over a 10-year saga, The Prophet (5.13d/5.14a R; 1,800ft) has developed a reputation as one of El Cap’s scariest and most dangerous free routes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that left to right: Alex Honnold, Connor Herson, and Tommy Caldwell take a celebratory selfie at the top of 'The Prophet' on El Cap. (Photo: Courtesy of Alex Honnold).

It has been revealed that my alarm goes off, but I’m already wide awake; I never sleep well before an early start. I’ve got half an hour to pull myself together before Alex gets here and we start hiking. As I choke down breakfast, I can’t help but wonder if I’m in over my head. Despite Alex and Tommy’s best reassurances, The Prophet scares me.

According to recent reports, established by Leo Houlding and Jason Pickles over a 10-year saga, The Prophet (5.13d/5.14a R; 1,800ft) has developed a reputation as one of El Cap’s scariest and most dangerous free routes. Indeed, it’s broken a few bones over the years, and to this day, Leo and Jason’s ground up attempt remains one of the boldest and most heroic chapters in El Cap’s history. Growing up, I always told myself that I’d never climb The Prophet. Maybe I’d rap into the A1 Beauty (the splitter crux pitch, rated 5.13d, though Leo, Sonnie Trotter, and Alex have all talked of upgrading it to 5.14a1) to try it, but the rest of the route was too dangerous for me—I don’t do dangerous stuff.

In a recent development, I wasn’t particularly surprised when Alex Honnold and Tommy Caldwell started trying The Prophet this season, but I watched their progress as a friend and spectator, not a potential suitor for the route. My own project on Leaning Tower was taking all my time this season.

On November 11, while eating breakfast and preparing for a day on my project, I ran into Alex and congratulated him on his send. He was hiking up that afternoon to belay Tommy, who was four days into his send push and trying the A1 Beauty. Alex offered to jumar and belay me on a ground-up push the next day, promising that the route was safer with his beta. I joked that I’d take him up if I couldn’t find a partner the next day for my project.

I had a very promising session on my project, but that afternoon, I was still partnerless for the following day, so I called up Alex to ask if his offer was still valid. In between Tommy’s redpoint goes on the A1, Alex called me back to tell me what gear I’d need. We planned to start climbing around 4:00 a.m. the following morning.

Packing up that evening, I felt wholly unprepared. I’d been sport climbing all summer and hadn’t done more than about six pitches in a day since spring. The only valley granite I’d touched this season was my overhanging, physical project on Leaning Tower, which was almost certainly a different style from the slabby, polished, and technical El Cap granite ahead of me. I’d need to re-adapt efficiently and quickly, working with a lower stamina threshold than I was used to.

Hiking up the following morning on November 12, Alex started breaking down the route for me. He told me how he and Tommy had cleaned all the pitches, how they ticked and recorded every gear placement. As I started leading the first few pitches, I realized just how helpful this was going to be: I took only the exact rack I’d need for each pitch, and I didn’t have to stress at all about beta or gear. I took Alex at his word about the relative safety of each section (a risky decision, I know…) and tried to turn my brain off to the fullest extent possible.

I settled into a sort of flow state; with the darkness obscuring any large runouts and Alex reassuring me of each gear placement ahead of me, I climbed calmly and intentionally over the lower pitches of the route. I couldn’t fathom Leo and Jason coming up here to find loose rock, grass-filled cracks, and no obvious route. It was certainly a far cry from my own experience on the freshly cleaned and ticked route. I remained relatively calm even over pitches four through six, the first few 5.13 pitches.

As we climbed higher and dawn broke, we saw Tommy above us; he’d not quite sent the night before, but he’d decided to spend another night on the wall and watch my attempt in the morning. With Tommy’s encouragement, I climbed the Guillotine Pitch (pitch eight, 5.13b), then the Devil’s Reacharound (pitch nine, 5.13a). Before long, I joined him at his portaledge at the base of the A1 Beauty just as the morning sun hit. What a perfect splitter it looked like, too—everything I could ever want in a pitch, at the very top of El Cap.

It has been revealed that the A1 Beauty sees direct sun from first light until sunset, and it bakes. It was already quite warm, and I figured it would only get warmer as the day progressed. Without much waiting, I racked up and started what I thought would be a beta sussing mission. A few moves in, I realized this attempt could be more than just that; with Tommy hanging on a static rope above me, telling me exactly what to do, I found myself through the low crux (~V8), then through the next section. As I got higher and higher, I tried to push down the feeling that I might just pull it off on this first attempt and instead focus on each move, each foothold, each gear placement. It felt perfect. Before I knew it, I was at the next anchor, absolutely thrilled.

As excited as I was about the A1, suddenly the route became much more intense. I was only two pitches below the summit. Two pitches from flashing the entire route in a day. Two pitches from an El Cap flash. The following pitch was easy enough, but the exit pitch intimidated me: a 13b boulder problem right off the belay, involving an insecure standup on poor footholds.

I climbed up to the boulder and back down to the belay a few times, feeling increasingly nervous. Eventually, I went for it: I placed the foot, took a deep breath, and stood. The foot held, and I excitedly reached for the next hold, which guards easier climbing to the top. I briefly lost focus, allowing a small voice to say, I’m doing it! It’s happening! The next thing I knew, my foot had slipped and I was hanging on the rope. My flash go was botched.

At that moment, I lost all perspective of the incredible morning of climbing I’d had; I was devastated. Half an hour later, topping out The Prophet after successfully climbing the pitch, I felt the most hollow I’ve felt upon topping out El Cap. Alex and Tommy joined me on top. As they packed their haulbag and portaledge, I couldn’t help but regret my missed opportunity.

Recent findings suggest that within a few minutes, however, I regained some perspective. It had been an incredibly memorable morning of climbing, and I’d still freed The Prophet ground-up in about seven hours. Only that morning, doing this would have been a dream come true, and I smiled a bit. I checked the time: 11:30 a.m. “Wow! I can drive home and meet my family in time for dinner!” I laughed and joked to Tommy and Alex.

Alex turned and gave me a wry smile. “You know, you could do a Double right now. Compared to The Prophet, Free Rider will probably feel pretty easy.”.

Tommy pitched in: “Yeah, I’d jug Free Rider this afternoon if you want!”.

It has been revealed that I stopped sorting my gear and stared. Great. I’m getting peer pressured by my heroes.

It has been revealed that among the rules I live by is that if Alex or Tommy offers something, I don’t turn them down. Especially a support mission on El Cap. As tired and emotionally drained as I was, I reminded myself just how much I’ve wanted to do the El Cap Double my entire life. I remembered topping out the free Nose-in-a-day last year, when I called every climber in the Valley to see if I could find a partner for a Double that day, to no avail. This sort of opportunity doesn’t come around particularly often. Even as I waffled about whether to go for it, the decision had been made. In a few hours’ time, I knew I’d be starting up Freeblast.

The climbing on Free Rider is significantly easier than on The Prophet, and I’d done most of the pitches when I freed the Salathé in 2022. I knew there would be little suspense about whether I’d be physically capable of sending it. However, I also knew I wasn’t in major walling shape, and besides, this would be far and away the most pitches I’ve climbed in a day. I remember watching the video of Tommy freeing the El Cap double back in 2005, where he nearly lost it at the Enduro Corner. I wondered if I was in for a similar bout.

The first few pitches on Free Rider went remarkably smoothly. Alex, still keen on supporting me, had jugged our day pack up the Heart Lines, which made Freeblast an absolute breeze. My feet were hurting, but I could feel the ibuprofen I’d pounded at the base starting to kick in. I settled into a flow, and pitch after pitch flew past. I felt remarkably fresh. With Tommy’s encouragement and psych, I was optimistic.

Around the Monster Offwidth (pitch 20 of 30 on Free Rider), darkness fell. I could feel the fatigue building; our pace slowed, but we kept moving. I was making a conscious effort to stay positive and cheerful, to act like I had endless energy in the hopes that I could fake that energy into existence.

In a recent development, when we reached the crux, I opted for the Teflon Corner instead of the Boulder Problem. I’d never tried the Boulder before, and I didn’t want my first attempt to be 40-odd pitches into the day. The Teflon went down on my first try, and before long, we were at the Enduro Corner. Tommy suggested that I skip the hanging belay at the end of the Enduro Corner and link it into the Round Table Traverse. I rolled my eyes, thinking that I’d be lucky to scrape my way up the Corner on its own, but to my surprise, I felt remarkably fresh. I reached the hanging belay and kept climbing, thankful to have cleared that last hurdle.

At 10:45 p.m., a little more than eight hours after starting Free Rider and 18.5 hours after starting up The Prophet, Tommy and I topped out to strong, cold winds. We didn’t stick around long to celebrate; already shivering, we swiftly packed and started running to stay warm on the hike down. As we got lower and warmed up, however, we slowed down and soaked in the unforgettable day we’d just had: around 45 pitches of climbing for a free El Cap Double!

Alex and Tommy both have families. They both had good reason to rush home ahead of the incoming storm instead of supporting some kid who wanted to try their project. And to be honest, I wouldn’t have blamed them if they didn’t want me to mooch off their hard work prepping The Prophet. There’s absolutely no way I could have done The Prophet ground up and in a day without the labor Tommy and Alex spent to find the route, clean loose rock, and find all the gear beta. After four days on the wall and away from his family, I would have completely understood if Tommy wanted to get home to his kids rather than go up El Cap a second time that day—especially with Tioga Pass imminently closing, which meant supporting me on Free Rider would lengthen his drive home by about an hour.

Nevertheless, their support that day exemplifies the exact values I love to see in climbing. This is the sport I want climbing to be: one where the giants, the biggest legends of the game, are generous enough to go out of their way to help younger up-and-comers. A sport where the younger generation is not seen as a fresh wave of competition but is instead embraced and mentored.

Industry observers note that not flashing The Prophet is certainly going to sting for a while. I still replay that moment on the exit pitch daily, and I’m sure I’ll always feel some regret about it. Still, the more I reflect on that day, the more Alex and Tommy’s support stands out to me. Every outing leaves us with a lesson or slightly shifted worldview. In 10 or 20 years, I’m confident that looking back on the El Cap Double will remind me that there is a world larger than my own climbing; that, like Tommy and Alex, I can make another climber’s entire season by simply offering them a few hours of my time and a bit of encouragement. As I grow and find my place in the climbing world, I can only hope to be as influential a mentor to future generations.

1It’s hard to guess after only one attempt, but I wouldn’t argue with 5.14a for that pitch! I also could see upper-end 5.13d, though.

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy.

The Gozney Arc XL pizza oven makes outdoor entertaining easy year-round, from backyard pizza parties to après-ski gatherings. (Photo: Courtesy of Gozney).

In a recent development, I wrote about my Gozney Arc XL pizza oven two summers ago, when it became the pie de resistance for using my backyard to get outside more (and for a suspicious number of new friends showing up at my house). More than a year later, I’m happy to report that the novelty hasn’t worn off. If anything, I love it more.

It has been revealed that one of my favorite ways to spend a Sunday afternoon, or unwind after a mountain bike ride, is inviting friends over for homemade pizzas. Everyone brings their favorite toppings, we experiment with different combinations, and dinner becomes an activity in itself. It’s dinner and a show, and everyone gets fed. And because we keep ours on a covered porch with adequate ventilation, pizza night doesn’t end when winter arrives. Après-ski pizza parties might actually be my favorite use for it.

Sources indicate that the Gozney Arc XL makes it ridiculously easy. It runs on propane (I use the same tank from my grill), reaches temperatures up to 950°F, and can cook a 16-inch pizza in as little as 60 seconds. Its lateral rolling flame distributes heat across the oven, so you don’t have to constantly rotate your pizza. The result is that perfectly blistered, chewy crust I usually associate with my favorite wood-fired pizza joints now in my own backyard.

Gozney makes several ovens, from more portable models to larger, more elaborate setups (many are also on sale right now). The Arc XL hits the sweet spot for me because it’s compact enough for our back patio, still with plenty of room to maneuver a full-size pizza.

In a recent development, you can make your own dough, buy Gozney’s mixes, or do what we do: keep Trader Joe’s premade pizza dough in the freezer so we’re always ready for an impromptu pizza night. One tip: a little semolina flour on your pizza peel helps the dough slide into the oven without sticking.

It has been revealed that my favorite toppings? Peaches, burrata, prosciutto, basil, and hot honey. Comment yours!

According to recent reports, learn from my mistake. When I first bought my Arc XL, I skipped the matching stand for a cheaper rolling cart from Amazon. It was a nightmare to assemble, felt flimsy, and looked terrible. I recently upgraded to the actual Gozney stand, and the difference is night and day. It’s sturdy, streamlined, easy to move, and designed to hold the oven securely. I should have trusted Gozney from the start.

In a recent development, the stand has a 4.8-out-of-5-star rating from 204 customer reviews, so apparently plenty of people knew something I didn’t. Worth the upgrade, especially while it’s on sale.

If you’re shopping for someone who already owns a Gozney, the brand’s pizza peels, dough trays, and other accessories make excellent gifts and are also on sale for Black Friday.

Food is fuel—the gas in our tanks that lets us get outside and play. But for dedicated foodies, cooking is about way more than calories. It’s about the experience, and sharing that experience with friends and family. Below, you’ll find 13 gifts that any chef will love, whether they’re an ultralight backpacker, a backyard BBQ master, or a cold coffee connoisseur. Bon appétit!

According to recent reports, the 10,000-BTU Zempire Stealth Jet Twin isn’t the most powerful camp stove we’ve ever tested, but it is the slimmest two-burner we’ve ever tested, making it a sweet gift for car campers who value trunk space and camp cuisine alike. Easy simmer controls and built-in igniters round this pick out as a major upgrade for campers still lugging WWII-era camp stoves that weigh as much as small sedans.

Both a firepit and a grill, Snow Peak’s Takibi is designed to be the centerpiece of camp life. While it’s a delight just to watch flames flicker in the portable stainless steel pit, the well-crafted, Japanese-made Takibi is an excellent charcoal grill. Pair it with Snow Peak camp cooking accessories to help your loved one build out the ultimate live-fire cooking setup.

We love the versatility of the Switch. It comes with an integrated pot for fast boiling à la Jetboil, but remove the pot and the prongs unfurl like those on a classic canister stove to accommodate bigger pots and pans. For backpackers who like to cook—but appreciate the convenience of dehydrated meals from time to time—the Switch is a nifty, thoughtful gift.

Sources indicate that when backpackers want to cut down on pack weight, they often opt for titanium cookware and accessories, as the metal offers an unbeatable strength-to-weight ratio. No one does titanium quite like Snow Peak. Smaller pieces, like Snow Peak’s iconic sporks, are a backpacker’s dream stocking stuffer, while drinkware and cooksets are destined to become prized possessions.

The compact and efficient Campstove 2+ can boil one liter of water in four and a half minutes, so it has morning coffee covered (you can also cook on it with some add-on components).

According to recent reports, this isn’t your usual camping stove, though. It runs on biofuel—either pellets you can purchase or sticks you find. And this stove has multiple uses: It can also charge your devices via an integrated USB port as well as function as a lamp with its included attachment.

Rare is the pan that can handle an open flame, an induction cooktop, and a piping-hot pizza oven. Crafted from a single piece of wrought iron, the non-toxic Solidteknics Iron Frypan is lighter than its cast-iron counterparts and features a long, slender, grabbable handle, making flipping flapjacks or searing steaks over a campfire a lot less strenuous. Adaptable, durable, and dependable, this pan is ready for adventurous weekends at camp and cozy weeknights at home.

It has been revealed that quince’s Hinoki Cutting Boards make ditching the microplastic-shedding chopping blocks of yesteryear a genuine pleasure. A Japanese cypress renowned for its almost citrusy fragrance, Hinoki is a soft, forgiving wood that will protect your precious knife blade. The wood is also naturally lightweight, making it easy to pack these boards into your camp kitchen bin.

Socks are always a slam-dunk stocking stuffer. But for foodies who grew up watching James Beard winner and Cooking Channel alum Emeril Lagasse say “Bam!” as he sprinkled seasoning into Creole and Cajun concoctions, these Stance socks earn the holiday equivalent of a Michelin star. Fun, hilarious, nostalgic, and comfortable to boot, these cotton crew socks are sure to earn a grin every time they’re dug out of the sock drawer. What more can we say but… BAM!

In a recent development, you might be wondering what the hell is Outside doing writing about a KitchenAid Tilt-Head Stand Mixer? It’s a fair question. And besides, the forest-green colorway and the natural woodgrain bowl make this mixer quite a thoughtful gift for the nature-loving baker, no? It’s on our holiday wish list, at least!

Sources indicate that being landlocked is no longer a problem for seafood-loving gourmands. Hog Island Oyster Company will ship boxes of Hog Island shellfish, accoutrements, and more nationwide, on ice, directly to your doorstep. If you’re looking for a gift that can hang out under a Christmas tree for a week, the California-based brand also sells a savory seasoning trio, subscription boxes, and gift cards.

Recent findings suggest that there are a million gizmos and gadgets out there for the espresso fanatics, the drip disciples, the press-and-plunge crowd. But what about the nitro lovers? Behold: the Cumulus Coffee Machine. An all-in-one robot for chilled coffee lovers that brings barista-grade bevies into the comfort of your own home, the machine has three settings that allow you to convert Cumulus pods into iced espresso, crisp cold brew, and creamy nitro. The nitro setting is particularly rad, as the Cumulus sources nitrogen from ambient air—no nitrogen cartridges required. And there’s no ice required, either, as the machine self-chills. #114285. How My First Multi-Pitch Climb Became a Midnight Barefoot Epic

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1341 w)

How My First Multi-Pitch Climb Became a Midnight Barefoot Epic

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1341 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Climbing

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • On July 4, 2026, Audrey Callaway climbed her first real multi-pitch: Diedre (5.8, 6 pitches) in Squamish, B.C.
  • Industry observers note that after first getting into the sport at a gym in Chicago, Callaway later moved to upstate Upcoming York near the Gunks.
  • Industry observers note that callaway wanted to share her experience to highlight the growing pains of “doing things poorly the first time”—and how the right partners ease those pains.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On July 4, 2026, Audrey Callaway climbed her first real multi-pitch: Diedre (5.8, 6 pitches) in Squamish, B.C. The catch? She didn’t start up pitch one until nearly 9 p.m., thus becoming voluntarily benighted in only the most literal sense of the term. “My story isn’t a disaster!” Callaway explains. “It’s about learning, the tenacity of a little psych, and extremely good manufacturer.”.

Industry observers note that after first getting into the sport at a gym in Chicago, Callaway later moved to upstate Upcoming York near the Gunks. Right now, she’s studying forestry at the University of Vermont. “I like trees, I like climbing, I like birds,” she indicates of her significant three hobbies. She’s mostly a boulderer and sport climber who wants to get more into trad climbing. She also works at a climbing gym.

Industry observers note that callaway wanted to share her experience to highlight the growing pains of “doing things poorly the first time”—and how the right partners ease those pains. Below, she shares her story and what others embarking on their first multi-pitch can learn from her experience.

It’s really cool to feel very bad at something again.

Sources indicate that I was planning to visit my girlfriend Lucy, who had been in Squamish for the whole summer. Then my best friend Will, who I grew up climbing with at the gym, told me he also happened to be going out to Squamish. I got there a few days before him and did a little bouldering.

When Will got there, he was even more psyched than I was. After bouldering all afternoon, we’re sitting around, playing chess and looking through Lucy’s guidebook when we saw a trad climb that looked so cool: Diedre (5.8, 6 pitches).

Sources indicate that it was 7 p.m., but the sun didn’t set until around 9 p.m. It was very spur of the moment. We’re just like, “We gotta do this thing.” So we promptly got all our stuff together.

In a recent development, we knew it was going to get dark. It’s not like it snuck up on us. But Lucy had a lot of experience. Will and I didn’t know how to trad climb at this point, although he learned later on that trip. So she’s carrying the team. Afterward, she told me she brought only a single rack so that she could share in our sense of adventure and “empathize with the uncertainty.”.

Recent findings suggest that first, we got super lost on the way there. We didn’t get to the base of the climb until like 8:45 p.m., but it was still super bright out.

It has been revealed that very swiftly, I realized how bad I was at rope management. I was in the middle, belaying Lucy, and we had two ropes. Routefinding is something that you take for granted when you’ve been climbing outside for a while. I was taking the path of most resistance. There was a pretty solid crack on really good terrain, but I’m newer to crack climbing, so I was not about to put my hands in there and trust that. Instead, I was doing this very sketchy 5.10 slab. Eventually, I started using the crack.

Sources indicate that we got up to the first belay and we’re all on top of each other because we don’t really know where to be. Nothing was unsafe, but it was very slow. Lucy started going up this 5.6 very runout slab. But I had looped a knot of rope around where I was belaying. I didn’t realize that until I’d fed out enough of the slack. So I kept shorting her like every five feet. I knew that there was totally a way to fix this, but I don’t know how.

In a recent development, then the sun set. That’s okay, because we had headlamps—but Lucy’s headlamp was dead. It was funny because before we started climbing, Lucy was like, “Guys, make sure you have your headlamps.” But then when we put them on, she’s like, “Can I actually borrow yours?”.

So she took mine, and now I was climbing in the dark on slab. It was very precarious, but beautiful. It felt so scary in the moment. But the town was right there, we’re on the most classic 5.8 ever, and we’re a hundred feet off the ground—it wasn’t actually that scary.

Will and I both had super competitive shoes on. It had been two hours at this point and we’re standing on this slab and our feet were killing us. Every time I left the belay, Will told me he “would lowkey start crying a bit” because he knew he’d have to climb soon, enduring more toe pain. So we both took off our shoes because it’s easier to climb barefoot. Now I was barefoot in the dark on this slab.

Every time we got to a new belay, we tried to make the system better. Lucy was just trying to climb, but we’re shorting her every time. Now Will was in the way. We were right on top of each other.

It has been revealed that none of these things were particularly hard challenges. If we knew what we were doing, we could have fixed any one of these problems in 30 seconds. I would get back up to Lucy and she would be like, “Why didn’t you just do this?” Then something else would come up.

According to recent reports, at one point, probably around 11:30 p.m., Will got a cam stuck. Lucy’s like, “Try wiggling it.” She told him to pull upward, but he stated it was literally impossible. Lucy lowered down and pulled it out, first try. There must have been times like this when Lucy was frustrated, but she never showed it. Will describes Lucy as the most patient person he’s ever met.

We got to the top at midnight. It was hypnotizing on the apron. The lights of town beneath us glowed surreally. I smoked my first cigarette at the top.

I remember walking back and it was really quiet. We got back on the road and our gear’s rattling and the moon’s out. It was so quiet and peaceful.

It was one in the morning when we got back to the campground by the Chief. We didn’t want to be disrespectful with a significant light, so we put a headlamp under this pickle jar we had. By the light of this pickle lamp, we ate pickles and cold canned minestrone and asked, “What are we gonna do tomorrow?”.

To really be benighted, I would say it has to sneak up on you. It kinda felt like it snuck up on me. Clearly, as a group we were aware it was about to happen. But I was surprised when all of a sudden it was dark and I had no headlamp and was climbing barefoot. It made me feel like a salamander, really in touch with the rock.

Recent findings suggest that lucy and I did another multi-pitch the next day, and since then I’ve done a couple two-pitch climbs in the Gunks when I got back to Latest York. I will probably do lots of really awesome multi-pitches in my lifetime that are beautiful and scenic with really hard climbing, but I’m never gonna have another one that bad. I’m never gonna have another first one.

According to recent reports, as told to Maya Silver. This story has been edited for length, structure, and clarity.

#114283. After a Scathing Report on the Dragon Bravo Fire, the Grand Canyon’s Superintendent Is Retiring

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (990 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outsideonline ↗ Open Full Page

After a Scathing Report on the Dragon Bravo Fire, the Grand Canyon’s Superintendent Is Retiring

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (990 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outsideonline

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that smoke rises from the Dragon Bravo Fire on the Grand Canyon’s North Rim in July 2025.
  • On November 23, Grand Canyon National Park Superintendent Ed Keable revealed his proposal to retire at the end of 2026, after more than six years overseeing the park.
  • Industry observers note that “As Geoffrey Chaucer wrote, ‘All good things must come to an end.’ So, too, my time at GRCA,” Keable wrote in a November 23 email to park employees obtained by Arizona Public Radio station KNAU.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that smoke rises from the Dragon Bravo Fire on the Grand Canyon’s North Rim in July 2025. The wildfire burned more than 145,000 acres and destroyed 114 structures, including the historic Grand Canyon Lodge (Photo: slovegrove/Getty).

On November 23, Grand Canyon National Park Superintendent Ed Keable revealed his proposal to retire at the end of 2026, after more than six years overseeing the park.

Industry observers note that “As Geoffrey Chaucer wrote, ‘All good things must come to an end.’ So, too, my time at GRCA,” Keable wrote in a November 23 email to park employees obtained by Arizona Public Radio station KNAU. In the email, he confirmed that his last day will be December 31 and that agency leaders are working to identify an acting superintendent to take over on January 1.

Keable’s announcement came just ten days after the Department of the Interior released a damning 65-page investigative report detailing how leadership failures, inadequate preparation, and communication breakdowns contributed to the devastating 2025 Dragon Bravo Fire, which destroyed 114 structures on the park’s North Rim, including the historic Grand Canyon Lodge.

The investigation drew on interviews with more than 70 people and a review of over 18,000 documents, including fire management intends and communication logs.

Keable’s retirement email made no mention of the Dragon Bravo Fire or the Interior Department’s investigative report.

“I have made this decision for very personal reasons,” Keable wrote.

Outside contacted Keable and the National Park Service for comment but did not receive a response as of the publishing of this story.

Recent findings suggest that A career government attorney, Keable spent 23 years in the Interior Department’s Office of the Solicitor, including eight years as assistant solicitor of general law, before his appointment in April 2020 during President Donald Trump’s first administration. He had no previous experience working for the National Park Service.

The Coalition to Protect America’s National Parks, an organization representing current and former park service employees, issued a statement on April 3, 2020, criticizing Keable’s selection the same day the NPS announced his appointment.

“Ed Keable is not qualified to manage and lead a complicated park such as the Grand Canyon,” Phil Francis, then-chair of the coalition, said in the statement.

In the appointment announcement, NPS Deputy Director David Vela praised Keable’s leadership abilities and cited his experience within the Interior Department as an asset to the park.

According to recent reports, sparked by lightning on July 4, 2025, the Dragon Bravo Fire burned more than 145,000 acres over nearly three months and cost an estimated $141 million to suppress, according to the federal report. Investigators concluded that “the most consequential drivers were not environmental,” finding that many of the challenges the NPS and firefighters encountered during the blaze were “foreseeable, preventable, and reflective of broader institutional issues.”.

In the report, investigators determined that “leadership roles did not align with expertise or decision making authority.” As the fire’s agency administrator, Keable was responsible for overseeing firefighting strategy and authorizing suppression tactics.

Recent findings suggest that under NPS guidelines, superintendents at wildfire-prone parks are expected to qualify for that role within two years of their appointment. Five years into his tenure, Keable still lacked that qualification, the report mentioned. Although qualified administrators were available locally, the park didn’t bring one in until July 30, nearly four weeks after the fire ignited.

Recent findings suggest that keable initially approved a strategy known as confine and contain, which involves keeping a wildfire within designated boundaries rather than extinguishing it entirely. The approach conflicted with 2025 federal guidance against managing wildfires for ecological benefit, though investigators indicated that Keable had not received that, the report noted.

Park leadership reaffirmed the strategy twice over the next five days, during which the fire breached planned containment lines.

“Continued authorization of the confine and contain strategy did not reflect awareness of changing conditions or escalating risk,” investigators wrote.

Communication failures also delayed firefighters’ efforts to slow the blaze using aerial fire retardant. Keable authorized retardant drops on July 13, once an earlier request from firefighters was clarified, but by then, the Grand Canyon Lodge had already burned.

Recent findings suggest that the report stopped short of assigning individual fault. “The Dragon Bravo Fire should be understood as a warning event,” the report stated. “The findings demonstrate outcomes were shaped less by tactical execution than by NPS systemic concerns related to authority, qualifications, and decision processes.”.

As Outside reported in April, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum suggested that full suppression might have prevented hundreds of millions of dollars in property losses, though wildland firefighters noted that the canyon’s steep terrain initially made ground operations unsafe.

The National Park Service advertised Keable’s position on November 24, with applications closing December 8 and an annual salary ranging from $162,740 to $228,000. Responsibilities include overseeing wildland firefighting, emergency medical services, and backcountry rescues.

According to recent reports, the job hunt comes at a pressing time for the national park. A devastating flash flood on August 29 destroyed trails and infrastructure along the Colorado River and led to three deaths. Facilities on the South Rim went without running water for nearly two months until the park restored water service to six lodges on November 20.

Industry observers note that among the next superintendent’s biggest challenges will be rebuilding the North Rim. Earlier this month, the park service concluded a public comment period on three preliminary redevelopment concepts for the area. Congress is also considering the North Rim Restoration Act, which would give the park service greater contracting flexibility to expedite reconstruction.

According to recent reports, sections of the fire-damaged North Rim reopened to visitors in May, but the August flash flood hindered reconstruction efforts, washing out trails and damaging bridges and critical infrastructure. The entire North Kaibab Trail and Cottonwood Campground remain closed, and Phantom Ranch’s lodging closure has been extended through January 31, 2027.

Your kids might not remember what was under the tree, but we promise they’ll never forget the nights spent under the stars with their family. Lucky for parents, outdoor gear is more family-friendly than ever. Think: tents you can stand up in, paddle boards that pack into a backpack, campsite games, passenger-friendly e-bikes, and so much more. These 12 adventure-ready gifts are for the families on your list who’d rather spend the weekend at the campsite, on the water, or on the bike path than on the couch with an iPad in hand.

Sources indicate that the best part of birding is that there’s no real age requirement or limit. It’s arguably one of the most accessible (and relaxing) ways for families to enjoy the outdoors. Psst…we have lots more birding gear recs where this came from.

Sources indicate that you don’t have to give up hiking if you’ve got little ones. It just takes some helpful gear to keep the adventure going strong. Add a hiking backpack carrier to your gear closet so it’s easy to get your kids on the trail. Backpack carriers are best for youngins under 5 years old or 55 pounds. Our favorite pick for longer hiking trails is the Deuter Kid Comfort Child Carrier, which fits like a backpacking pack and includes tons of features to make hiking with kids much easier. And if you’re lucky, you just might squeeze some trail naps in.

Camp games, anyone? ENO’s latest TrailFlyer game is like bags (or cornhole, as we call it in the Midwest) but designed for camping. It packs down into a small carrying case and takes just a few minutes to set up. Wrap the adjustable straps around a tree trunk or sturdy anchor point, stake out the feet, and start tossing.

Industry observers note that our family has put the heavy-duty Victory Patio Blanket to use as a play area for our crawling baby at camp, and we’ve taken it to plenty of beach days and park picnics. The underside is coated in a thick, waterproof material that keeps moisture and dirt from seeping through. You can also toss it in your tent to make a cozier floor or dress up your campsite with an outdoor rug.

Good luck wrapping a kayak (or fitting it in your garage). Skip the bulky gift for the packable and portable inflatable ISLE Switch 3. This hybrid SUP-kayak fits in a backpack with everything you need to hit the water, including a paddle, pump, and inflatable kayak seats. It’s the perfect adventure gift for a family who loves getting out on the water.

Sources indicate that keep it old school with this point-and-shoot camera that’s perfectly nostalgic. Don’t let its lack of a screen fool you. This screen-free digital camera is rechargeable and can capture up to 500 photos per charge. It also offers several built-in filters—standard, vintage, analog, and black-and-white—that you can swap with the push of a button. Bonus: it comes with a microSD card already inside, so you’ve got room for around 2,000 photos from day one.

Sources indicate that if you want to take the littlest adventures with all their gear along, this wagon makes it easy. It works three ways: as a wagon for hauling, as a stroller with two 5-point safety harness seats, and as a car seat carrier with the included adapter (car seat not included).

It has been revealed that the Wrangler Deluxe holds up to 110 pounds and brings the tough, trail-ready spirit Jeep is known for, with all-terrain puncture-proof airless tires and swivel front wheels for easy maneuvering. A removable cooler bag holds up to 16 cans, and the wagon also has a UV-blocking canopy, pull-down shades, a cup holder, a parent organizer, and multiple storage pockets. When it’s time to pack up, it folds compactly.

Industry observers note that cozy up around the campfire with the ones you love in this two-seater camp chair. Its low-profile, reclined design puts you at just the right height for roasting s’mores and soaking up the fire’s warmth. And for a chair that fits two (or three if you’ve got a kiddo on your lap), it packs down surprisingly small.

We can’t mention s’mores without plugging our favorite roasting sticks. These reusable, telescoping metal roasting forks make great stocking stuffers. Our set has lasted through years of camping, and we love using them not only for marshmallows but also for hot dogs, sausages, and the occasional Twinkie.

In a recent development, due for a latest family cooler? Keep beers, bubbly water, juice boxes, and everything in between ice-cold in the Hydro Flask 15L Carryout Soft Cooler. It’s easy to carry and easy to clean, which makes it a go-to for camping trips, road trips, soccer tournaments, and backyard grill-outs. Don’t worry about scratches, broken buckles, or dings, either: Hydro Flask offers a lifetime warranty.

Who needs a minivan when you’ve got the Aventon Abound LR? This cargo e-bike is made for family adventures in the city and beyond, featuring an extra-long rear rack that fits two kids (or one kiddo plus panniers full of gear). Hills are no match for its powerful 750W motor, and you can ride up to 60 miles on a single charge. We opted for the smaller Abound SR since we’re a “one-and-done” family, but the LR is a great upgrade if you have more kids and gear to haul.

Industry observers note that give the gift of camping! Hipcamp takes the stress out of snagging a campsite before it sells out. Its database of private land available for rent connects you with one-of-a-kind stays—from tent sites on farms and vineyards to cabins, glamping tents, and treehouses. All you have to do is dream up your family’s perfect night under the stars.

The perfect family camping tent doesn’t exis—oh wait, there’s The North Face Wawona 6. It’s tall enough to stand up in, sleeps six, features tons of interior pockets, and has color-coded poles to make setup a breeze. Speaking of a breeze, oversized mesh windows help ventilate the tent on muggy summer nights. The best part? A huge vestibule that works like a front porch, giving you a shady and dry spot to kick back in camp chairs in hot or rainy weather.

  • In a recent development, giving someone a Halo Collar 5 is like offering them an infinite series of fenced backyards—except the fences weigh nothing and the backyards appear wherever you want them.
  • You can set up an unlimited number of wireless virtual fences that work everywhere: at home, traveling, and even off the grid.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Dog people: We all know a few. You might be one yourself. Fortunately, dog lovers are easy to spot—and fun to shop for. After all, nothing delights a dog person more than a gift that will keep their pets safer, healthier, and happier. These seven picks will level up your favorite dog lover’s every adventure, from the backyard to the trailhead.

In a recent development, giving someone a Halo Collar 5 is like offering them an infinite series of fenced backyards—except the fences weigh nothing and the backyards appear wherever you want them. This GPS-powered virtual fence system lets dogs roam within specific boundaries, granting them the freedom to explore while still keeping them safe.

You can set up an unlimited number of wireless virtual fences that work everywhere: at home, traveling, and even off the grid. Plus, the AlwaysOn GPS system provides live tracking 24 hours a day, with location updates coming in 20 times per second for total peace of mind. Dog lovers can trust the Halo Collar 5 will keep their pups exactly where they need to be, thanks to Precision+ GPS technology that’s three times more accurate than any other GPS dog fence.

According to recent reports, when wearing the Halo Collar 5, pooches learn to stay within the virtual fence through feedback delivered wirelessly to the collar: A customizable set of vibrations, sounds, and/or static alerts dogs when they reach the boundary. Renowned dog trainer Cesar Millan helped develop this positive-reinforcement training system. The collar fits dogs 10 pounds and up, with neck sizes ranging from 8.5 to 30.5 inches. The battery holds 40-plus hours of charge and easily recharges in about an hour. And since the collar has a waterproof rating up to three feet, dogs can drink, swim, and romp in the rain with no problems.

Sources indicate that get the Halo Collar 5 at its lowest price ever: $419. The sale ends on December 2.

Industry observers note that there’s a better way than hiding that ugly wire dog crate behind the furniture. Way better. Part doggie haven, part stylish side table, this beautiful crate deserves a place of honor. The bentwood structure offers a secure den with holes for ventilation and light. An optional acrylic gate stows away neatly within the crate’s roof when you don’t need it. Available in multiple sizes to accommodate most pups.

It has been revealed that A dog’s bad breath might be more than just annoying—it could be a sign of dental disease. Most dogs have too much tartar and plaque buildup, contributing to that infamous doggie breath. But you don’t need a toothbrush: You need dental dog treats. These bendable, rawhide-free treats are designed to clean Fido’s teeth down to the gumline, leading to 47 percent less tartar and 40 percent less plaque accumulation. Available in a variety of sizes and flavors.

Recent findings suggest that after a big adventure—or just a romp in the woods—every dog deserves a comfy place to rest in camp. This travel dog bed is just the ticket: It rolls up and packs with integrated compression straps and a handle, making it easy to tote from home to the campsite and anywhere else in between. Two layers of enhanced memory foam provide support and comfort, while a waterproof bottom and protective zip liner shield it from whatever Mother Nature throws your way.

The only downside to your dog joining you on your adventures: muddy pawprints all over the car. Stop the mess with this durable, waterproof backseat cover. The 100 percent recycled polyester shield works in either bench or hammock mode to keep dogs safe for the ride. (Hammock mode includes a mesh window for airflow and visibility.) Stuffer cleats, loops, and a grippy coating keep the cover in place while maintaining access to seatbelts. The best part: You can clean it with a shake (though it’s machine washable, too).

Some dogs have separation anxiety from their owners—or is it the other way around? Either way, this smart dog camera can help. The Furbo automatically tracks your pup around the house, providing a video feed via smartphone app, and lets you talk to your pet in real time. Even better, the camera can pop out a treat whenever your dog needs a pick-me-up. The optional Furbo Nanny AI subscription service adds personalized daily reports, updates, and emergency alerts.

Staying hydrated on the go is as important for your dog as it is for you. This ultralight travel dog bowl makes it easy to give your pooch a drink in the park, on the trail, and in camp. The durable, leakproof coated-nylon bowl holds up to 16 ounces yet weighs less than an ounce and packs down small enough to disappear in your backpack or pocket.

In a recent development, the Halo Collar™ is the most advanced GPS dog fence ever created. Co-founded by Cesar Millan, the patented system combines wireless smart fencing, smart training, real-time GPS tracking, and activity monitoring into one easy-to-use smart collar. Halo’s proprietary GPS and GNSS location technology helps keep dogs safe while giving them the freedom to explore. Halo protects more than 500,000 dogs across the United States each day. For more information, visit halocollar.com.

26 Black Friday Deals on Editor-Tested Ropes, Packs, Shoes, and More

  • Industry observers note that if you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission.

  • In this economy, climbers can’t afford to pass up a good deal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that if you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy.

(Photo: Courtesy Black Diamond, Ocun, Scarpa, and Trango).

In this economy, climbers can’t afford to pass up a good deal. Unless you’re crafty and have a sewing machine—not to mention a home welding kit—we imagine there are a few things you could use. Most of the deals we outline below can be found at Backcountry, at REI, and at specific manufacturers like Black Diamond.

Backcountry released its Black Friday Sale early on November 20, with deals up to 60% off. We found some of the best deals on climbing shoes there. Competing outdoor retailer REI launched a Holiday Sale on November 13 with up to 25% off discounts that we expect to endure through Cyber Monday. However, if you’re shopping in person, keep in mind that the co-op is closed on Black Friday itself for its annual #OptOutside campaign.

On the brand side, Black Diamond has been running an outlet sale more or less all month with up to 50% off past styles (mostly apparel, but some hardgoods). Black Diamond is offering a Holiday Sale through November 30 with up to 25% off. On November 27, it shifts into deeper Black Friday and Cyber Monday deals of up to 60% off. We found some steals on editor-recommended gear at BD you won’t want to miss.

As you head into the discount madness, here are a couple Black Friday/Cyber Monday shopping tips for climbers:.

Looking to build out your climbing shoe quiver? Is your go-to pair beyond the point of resole or repair? Ready to graduate to a more performance-oriented design? This is your moment. You may be thinking: But I’m not going to be climbing much for the next few months. I’ll just wait.

Real ones know that would be a grave error. Come February or March, you will still need newly introduced shoes. But chance are, they’ll be full price. Plus, if you plan ahead and invest now, you can spend the winter breaking them in around the gym. Here are a few standout Black Friday climbing deals on rock and approach shoes to consider below.

Industry observers note that if your footwork repertoire involves pockets and micro edging, the La Sportiva Miura VS Climbing Shoe is among the best. Last year, we chose the Miura VS as the best tech shoe out there. With an aggressive downturn and semi-stiff, low-profile toe box, this shoe is perfect for precision climbing up slab and narrow cracks. Note that VS means this shoe uses a Velcro closure.

La Sportiva’s Katana is an awesome technical shoe for edging and beyond. Note that the men’s version is stiffer than the women’s version. This shoe is great for precision placements on slab, narrow cracks, and steep routes. After a buddy gifted me his slightly too small Katanas, I had them resoled and have been loving them indoors and out. You can also check out our review of the Katana here.

With great grip and breathability, these approach shoes strike a near-perfect balance between nimble hiking and climbing performance—without the weight. That’s why we selected the TX2 Evo as our top pick for a lightweight approach shoe last year. We also love that La Sportiva crafts this pair with recycled materials and a sole designed for easy repairs. This is one of the best Black Friday climbing deals out there if you need a good approach shoe.

We haven’t seen deals this pervasive on shoes in a while. All but ONE of the dozen pairs we gave top billing in our Fall 2026 Shoe Guide are marked down right now at Backcountry. (The only shoe that evaded discounts is the Scarpa Furia Air, our top pick for a “soft/high-feedback” shoe.) You can read our testers’ thoughts on each shoe in our guide, and see the deals on each shoe and what it’s best for below.

The Red Chili Voltage: “a sleeper classic—a tautly crafted, downturned, asymmetrical performance sport shoe with a solid crossover into bouldering.”.

Scarpa VSR LV: “Across a range of styles and grades, testers praised the shoe’s precision on tiny footholds and its power on steep terrain.”.

La Sportiva Ondra Comp: “Maybe the best toe-hooking shoe I have encountered—ever.”.

Mad Rock D2 One: “… I can safely call these the most versatile, ideal for both bouldering and sport.”.

Butora Ibex: “Hardcore boarders, boulderers, and comp climbers will love it, though I also found it versatile for vertical edging.”.

Evolv Phantom Pro: “… offers massive-time driving and grabbing power paired with a velvety, forgiving footbed and single-strap, sock-like closure.”.

Ocún Jett S: “For a ‘narrow’ slipper, the Jett S still has enough lateral stretch to accommodate wide feet, with a comfy last great for long gym sessions—both bouldering and sport.”.

La Sportiva Mantra: “With a significant downcamber and mild asymmetry, the sensitive and pared-down Mantra is great for grabbing big, smeary holds.”.

Evolv Zenist Pro: “The Zenist Pro stands out for its edging and all-around prowess, and is perhaps not as smeary or grabby as the marketing would have you believe.”.

Scarpa Generator Mid: ““The Generator Mid’s substantial toe box was adept at rand smearing in a sustained corner crack and for the wide stuff, but boxy and insensitive in thin jams.”.

Update: This shoe has sold out at Backcountry since we first published this deals round-up.

Scarpa Blackbird: “Over months of testing, the Blackbird has certainly lived up to its hype and its price … The edging power on the Blackbird is off the charts, with the best support and stability on square-cut edges of any shoe I’ve worn.”.

Beyond shoes, there’s a lot more climbing gear on sale out there during Black Friday. Ropes, hardware, and more are all marked down 20% or more. Here are our top editor-tested picks.

Industry observers note that most climbers care about the planet. We can do our part in a lot of ways, one of which is buying more planet-friendly gear. Edelrid manufactured this 70m rope with over 40% renewable materials, leveraging a bio-based polyamide in part made from castor oil. This is the first synthetic rope of its kind that relies less heavily on fossil fuels. Of course, the rope has to work, too, and in tests, we found it held up well. It feeds well and proved kink-resistant in our tests. We dubbed it the best eco-friendly cord in our 2025 rope guide.

Sources indicate that we tested Mammut’s Alpine Core Protect Rope and called it one of the safest ropes we’d ever used. It also held up remarkably well after significant abuse in the field. By weaving burly aramid fibers into its core, this innovative rope from Mammut helps resist cutting. And right now, you can snag it at 20% off.

Using the same cam-assisted blocking that makes the Grigri the safer choice over an ATC or other devices, the NEOX innovates with an integrated wheel that makes feeding out slack when lead belaying faster and smoother. Petzl also engineered the NEOX with recycled materials to reduce its environmental impact. We’ve used it for rock, gym, and ice climbing and we’re big fans.

Sources indicate that I have been loving the Black Diamond Solution Hoody as a light fall belay jacket and even for cold rock climbing when I’m too chilly to shed my jacket. The Solution manages to be super lightweight, movement-friendly, and breathable, yet warm. This is largely because the specific PrimaLoft insulation used in this jacket is made with technology developed by NASA for astronauts. Here on earth, it also works great. It honestly does feel like being wrapped in warm air. The pocket real estate is also generous, and it’s nice that the whole thing packs into the left hand pocket so you can easily stash it in your pack.

A chance to save on cams? We’ll take it. Snag one (or a few) of this Black Diamond #.5 to enhance your rack for fast and light missions.

Our top all-around harness of Fall 2026, the Solution uses what Black Diamond dubs Contour Edge Technology for the waist and leg loops, meaning they’re more rigid in the middle, but flexible and soft at the edges for increased comfort. One of our testers found that this made for a climbing harness with “fantastic” hip support. It didn’t cause any uncomfortable pressure or distracting pain points on his body, steadfastly supporting him during 10-hour days on the wall.

One of our editors’ favorite gifts for this holiday season, Trango’s REAL Chalk is better for humans and the planet. This seawater-sourced chalk comes in 50g, 250g, or 500g bags. Makes for a great stocking stuffer—or stock up for yourself for 2027.

Recent findings suggest that I bought a BD Momentum Full-Body Harness in 2018 or 2019 and am still using it today. It’s been through years of indoor and outdoor climbing with both of my kids. It’s user-friendly, too—a four-year-old can handle putting it on themselves. When my son finally outgrows his next spring, it’s in good enough shape that we will pass it down to another climbing family. This is a great time to save on a kids’ harness that will last until your kid outgrows it.

Industry observers note that perhaps the most hyped carabiner of 2026 (if there is such a thing as carabiner hype), the Magnetron returned by popular demand a few months ago. After rapidly going out of stock, what’s been billed as “Alex Honnold’s favorite carabiner” is now back in inventory—and on sale. The biggest boon of this cult-favorite gear is that you can never forget to lock it, thanks to an automatic magnetic locking mechanism. However, it’s not great for ice/alpine climbing and can be a tad difficult to operate for smaller hand sizes. I personally have a small hand and find it easy to use and love it. But you can read our full thoughts here.

One of our top ice tool picks this winter, the Black Diamond Hydras offer an impeccably balanced swing, ultra-precise pick, and a high degree of modularity make the Black Diamond Hydra our tool of choice for moderate and vertical ice. Interchangeable screw-on head weights let us dial in balance for any terrain, and the razor-thin picks—2.5 millimeters at the tip versus a 3- to 3.5-millimeter industry average—place like a dream. Read more about the Hydras in our Winter Gear Guide.

According to recent reports, our best all-around helmet of Fall 2026, the Black Diamond Vision offers the best of both worlds when it comes to comfort and weight. Made from mostly foam, with a plastic, ABS hardshell covering a portion of the top of the helmet, the Vision is impressively light at 215 grams.

Industry observers note that after quickly burning through Black Diamond Crack Gloves (that broke within a few months while climbing an indoor crack), I ordered a pair of these Ocún gloves a couple years ago and have loved them ever since. They are easy to put on, simple to clip to a back gear loop of your harness (I keep them clipped under my chalkbag), comfortable, and super durable on sandstone, granite, and human-made cracks alike.

According to recent reports, searching for more Black Friday deals? Check out the Climbing deals hub here.

15 Camping Gifts for People Who Would Rather Be in a Tent

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy.

(Photo: Courtesy REI, Black Diamond, Stio, Gozney, Kelty).

Some people book a luxury hotel for the weekend. Others would rather throw a tent in the car and figure out where they’re sleeping later. If you have one of the latter on your holiday shopping list, we’ve got you covered. Below are the best camping gifts that will make their time outside a bit more comfortable—even if they swear they don’t care about that. From the practical gear they’ll use on every trip to the fun extras that let them have their creature comforts, these presents will have them plotting their getaway ASAP.

A good pair of hiking socks is always appreciated, but these come with a little extra feel-good factor. Made with 70 percent organic cotton and a cushioned footbed, Conscious Step socks are comfortable enough for long days on the trail (or lazy ones around camp). Even better, purchases support the National Parks Conservation Association, which works to protect America’s public lands.

Sources indicate that this interactive water bottle doubles as an excuse to plan their next big camping trip. It comes with 63 illustrated, water-resistant stickers representing every national park in the U.S., so they can track where they’ve visited as they go. Since it’s a Nalgene, it’s also durable and featherlight, perfect for hanging from backpacks and gear bags.

In a recent development, this is the ideal gift for the person who considers coffee a nonnegotiable, regardless of how far they’ve wandered from civilization. This compact brewer is roughly the size of a thermos and makes hot coffee and cold brew concentrate in minutes. Simply add finely ground coffee and hot or cold water, let it brew, then use the hand press to dispense a concentrated shot into the included carafe. With no plugs and no charging required, they can throw it in their bag and go.

Recent findings suggest that camp chairs are great, but they’re not always the easiest things to lug around. This compact stool weighs just 1.2 pounds, folds down to 7.5 inches, and has a swiveling seat that lets you turn without having to pick up and reposition the whole thing. It supports up to 260 pounds, too, which is impressive for its size.

This is a particularly useful piece of gear for any camper who wants to cut down on what they’re carrying. Hydrapak’s collapsible flask has a built-in filter that removes common waterborne bacteria and parasites, allowing hikers to refill from water sources along the trail. It weighs just 4.1 ounces and packs completely flat when empty. It’s a great option for biking, hiking, paddling, and even traveling through sketchy airport bathrooms.

A headlamp is one of those camping essentials you don’t fully appreciate until you’re stumbling around camp in the dark. The Storm delivers up to 550 lumens with adjustable brightness, three different colored modes (red, blue, and green) to preserve night vision, and a waterproof-rated IPX7 construction that can handle rain and snow. It also has a lock mode to prevent it from accidentally turning on in your pack and draining the batteries before you even reach camp.

It has been revealed that if you want your family and friends to experience comfort in camp, look no further than this hammock. The kit has everything someone needs to set up between two trees, including polyester straps and iron carabiners. The Portable Hammock has a weight capacity of 551 pounds and it exhibits both the toughness and user-friendliness that Jeep is known for: It’s made from durable nylon and conveniently packs away into a built-in pouch that doubles as a pocket when the hammock is set up.

Industry observers note that there are hundreds of camp slippers on the market, but few are as truly warm or versatile as Glerups. Made from 100 percent natural wool, they’re naturally temperature-regulating and odor-resistant, so feet stay comfortable without getting swampy. The slip-on design makes them easy to kick off tent-side, while the rubber sole handles dirt, mud, and slippery moss with ease.

Finicky sleepers will love this sleeping bag. The Kelty Eclipse skips the traditional zipper in favor of a clever wraparound design that campers spread out when they’re hot or cocoon themself when they’re cold. What it lacks in zippers it makes up for in thoughtful details, including a self-sealing foot vent, oversized hood to keep pillows in place, and internal pockets. It’s also rated to 15 degrees Fahrenheit, so it’s built for more than just balmy summer nights.

Industry observers note that A good outdoor blanket earns its keep in just about every situation, and Yeti’s Lowlands is designed to handle more than one night under the stars. Its waterproof, puncture-resistant bottom keeps damp ground from seeping through, while the cushioned top provides a comfortable place to sit, stretch out, or let the dog settle in. Roll it up for transport, then bring it out for everything from picnics to beach days to tailgates.

In a recent development, if their cooking kit is just a recycled takeout container and one random spork, please get them this Gerber set. The 16-piece set includes a saute pan, stock pot, hot pad, and tableware for four people, giving them everything they need to make and serve a proper meal without cobbling together a kitchen from mismatched gear. When they’re finished, everything nests together for easy packing until the next time they need it.

These are the pants they’ll put on once at camp and have absolutely no interest in taking off, especially in colder temps. The Fernos pair a cozy insulated interior with a water-resistant exterior, making them ideal for chilly mornings, lounging around the campsite, or layering over a base layer when snow starts to fall. In other words, they’re very durable sweatpants.

Industry observers note that this is about as close as campers can get to bringing their mattress into the woods. The 3.9-inch memory foam pad is thick, supportive, and genuinely comfortable—more proper bed than half-deflated sleeping pad situation. It’s not designed for backpacking (don’t try to carry this on a thru-hike), but it’s portable enough to toss in the car for weekend camping trips. It rolls up tightly for storage and transport and self-inflates when unrolled, making set-up a breeze.

One of the best things about Luno’s car camping mattresses is that they’re not reserved for people with tricked-out 4x4s. The Air Pro is designed to fit a wide range of vehicles, with custom-fit options for dozens of makes and models. This particular kit includes a luxe inflatable mattress, air pump, fitted sheet, pillow, and window screen set that turns their backseat into a dreamy place to sleep. Simply put in their car’s year, make, and model and choose their window size for the gift of spontaneous overnights and long road trips.

Industry observers note that this is for the camp chef who thinks camping dinner should involve way more than hot dogs and s’mores. The Gozney Tread is a portable pizza oven that heats up to 950°F and cooks a delicious pie in about a minute. Its compact design makes it shockingly easy to transport and it runs on propane, so they won’t need to fuss with building a fire. Sure, it’s a bit of a splurge for the campsite, but the lucky recipient will have no trouble convincing their camping buddies it’s worth the extra trunk space.

It has been revealed that all campers know that a tent you can properly stand up in is the gift that keeps on giving. The Aurora Highrise has near-vertical walls and a roomy interior that comfortably accommodates up to six people, making it a good pick for families or groups who don’t love sleeping elbow-to-elbow. Large windows and doors let in plenty of light and airflow, while Nightlight Pockets let headlamps and flashlights cast an ambient glow. There’s also a generous vestibule for stashing muddy boots, camping chairs, and anything else that needs protection overnight.

The author climbing in Significant Cottonwood Canyon in northern Utah. Her most prevalent intrusive thought? The rope is going to cut. (Photo: Casey Coleman).

Warning: The following piece includes several examples of intrusive thoughts, including acts of violence in a climbing setting. It does not constitute treatment or medical advice, and is not intended for individuals with Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD).

According to recent reports, have you ever been 50 feet or so off the deck when an intrusive thought suddenly disrupts your climbing? Maybe it’s about something you forgot to do—lock your doors, extinguish your campfire, or put your dog outside. For a lot of us, it’s fear-based: I’m going to deck and break my ankles. Sometimes, it’s more sinister: I should let go of the brake strand or I should untie my knot.

Intrusive thoughts are more common than you might think. A 2014 study across 13 countries found that 93.6% of university students reported experiencing intrusive thoughts at least once during the previous three months. Stress is known to be one of the most common triggers of intrusive thoughts. So in a sport with an entire cottage industry around psychologically outsmarting the fear response, could intrusive thoughts be even more likely to emerge?

While no studies exist on intrusive thoughts among climbers, a fresh book touches upon these unwanted notions that sometimes prey upon our minds. In Get a Grip, psychotherapist-climber Joel Robertson, MA MBACP, and coach Louis Parkinson guide climbers toward adopting a healthier mindset. They tackle constructively reframing comparisons to other climbers and setting realistic goals. Ultimately, they show climbers that we are not the equivalent of our thoughts—even the unwelcome, unpleasant, or truly intrusive ones.

“We are not our thoughts, and our thoughts are not objective truth,” Robertson notes.

After giving Get a Grip a read, we asked our readers to tell us about some of the strangest intrusive thoughts they’ve experienced in climbing on Instagram. From the innocuous (Did that fart come with a price?) to the dark (What if my belayer dies and I fall?), 119 climbers responded with fears they’ve had to ignore on the wall.

Recent findings suggest that A few climbers shared intrusive thoughts about their belayer. What if they stopped paying attention—or passed out? Or more disturbingly: “What if my boyfriend decides he wants to murder me right now and just lets me fall?” (Sadly, that’s not totally unfounded.) Only one belayer shared an urge-based intrusive thought about taking their climber off belay—and jumping off the wall.

Perhaps that climber experienced what’s known in French as “l’appel du vide,” or “the call of the void.” One researcher describes this phenomenon as “fleeting, involuntary urges to engage in dangerous actions, most often in situations involving heights or other perceived risks.”.

Most of the intrusive thoughts centered, unsurprisingly, on gear failure and falling. Did I forget to tie in properly? What if the rope cuts (my personal recurring intrusive thought)? And what does a factor 2 fall feel like?

Some expressed anxieties about wildlife on the wall. A few climbers worried about spiders and bees lurking in cracks. They envisioned mountain goats knocking them off the route and rattlesnakes looming on ledges.

Others shared intrusive urges: Skip every clip, remove your Grigri, just jump. Only one climber said they didn’t have any such thoughts: “Climbing is the one thing that quiets the intrusive thoughts with any sort of reliability.”.

With all of these ruminations externalized, I wondered whether we might be more likely to have intrusive thoughts while engaged in the sometimes high-stress activity of climbing. “I would say the process of climbing is one that may be affected by intrusive thoughts more than others,” Robertson indicates. Beyond prevalence, coping with these thoughts on a high-stakes climb can present more of a challenge. You can’t always fully stop what you’re doing to refocus your mind.

“While climbing, I think intrusive thoughts may be more noticeable, feel more difficult to manage, and pose more potential risk to physical safety, as compared with other pursuits that are less intensive, require less focus, and/or have us in situations of less physical risk,” Robertson notes.

So for the climbers who battle these internal distractions, what should we do when unwanted ruminations enter our minds?

In Get a Grip, Robertson and Parkinson outline a three-step process for dealing with all varieties of intrusive thoughts.

Most importantly, don’t panic at the thought you’re having. Frantically trying to eradicate it from your mind might backfire. The first step? Recognize what’s entered your mind. “Acknowledge the thought and listen to it,” Robertson recommends. ”Don’t try and banish the thought.”.

Sometimes, you might be having the thought for a reason. After all, anxiety about whether you tied in harks back to a long-time complacency trap in climbing: Forgetting to properly tie your knot.

According to recent reports, “Listen to the thought and see if it’s got any wisdom,” Robertson advises. For example, check your tie-in knot, if that’s what you’re worried about. Call down to your belayer and ask them to watch you. Or evaluate that last cam—and re-place it more securely or add a second piece—if ripping gear is what’s haunting your mind.

If you’re having an intrusive thought about something you can’t do anything about right now—like whether you forgot to turn off the oven at home—the goal is to manage the thought until you can do something about it, like texting your roommate to check the stove or until you can finish the route and get home.

In a recent development, then tell the thought, “I’ve heard you and I’ve acknowledged you. I’m putting you to the side.”.

Next, move forward. “Decide on a thing that you are going to think about now instead,” Robertson explains.

In a recent development, most importantly, redirect your focus to something specific. So it’s not, “Now I’m going to focus on climbing this route,” or “Okay, time to think about something else.” Rather, it’s, “I’m going to imagine exactly how that crimp up there feels on my right fingers,” then put your hand on it. Robertson states it’s about “deliberately choosing to focus on things that aren’t the unhelpful intrusive thought.”.

Recent findings suggest that an important thing to remember and accept is that your intrusive thought is probably not just going to disappear altogether. “It’s going to come back, but that’s fine,” Robertson explains. “Just know that it’s a process.” Try not to fret about or dread the prospect of the thought returning. Just keep acknowledging, refocusing, and moving up the wall.

In a recent development, what if you’re having an intrusive thought as a belayer versus as the climber? Robertson claims to apply the same logic. But if it’s truly a distracting thought, it might be best to ask your climber to get to a safe stance (e.g., clip and take, or gain a ledge) while you regain your full concentration on belaying. Pause, do some breathing work, acknowledge, and redirect, Robertson advises.

It has been revealed that since stress can lead to intrusive thoughts, and climbing can be stressful, Get a Grip highlights the importance of distinguishing between the good kind of stress and the bad kind of stress. Trad climber Hazel Findlay reflects on this in the book as well.

With distress, you feel out of control—and you’re not having any fun. Maybe you started up a route that is too far outside your limit. Or perhaps conditions are taking a turn for the worse and you’re trying to push through anyway. If you’re distressed, it might be best to back off, change course, or reconsider your approach if possible.

In the case of eustress, Robertson says you might feel some fear and not calm, but it’s more of a butterflies-in-your-stomach vibe, than a panicked “What have I gotten myself into?” situation. “It feels fun; it feels exciting,” Robertson says.

Sources indicate that to seek eustress and avoid distress, Parkinson recommends making accurate risk assessments based on your past experiences before committing to a climb. Think back through all of the precautions you’re taken—partner checks, researching the route, trusting your belayer. Then conjure up past analogous experiences of eustress that you powered through. “I recommend thinking back on similar situations with similar levels of fear that you’ve survived successfully,” Parkinson indicates. “I do that for myself when I get scared on something.”.

Sources indicate that parkinson will acknowledge the fear or intrusive thought, then talk himself through it: “This feels scary, but it feels scary in a really similar way to something I’ve done before. And I managed to do that, so I’m going to carry on with this level of fear for a bit longer if I can.”.
